You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapFrontier Models as Research Engines: VP ≠ VNP, Protein Design and 948 Kernel BugsVP ≠ VNP, posted by two labs: An Anthropic GitHub repo reportedly contains a proof by an internal Claude research model that VP ≠ VNP. This is the algebraic analogue of P vs NP, posed by Valiant in 1979, and implies that polynomials such as the permanent lack small circuits over every field (@kimmonismus, repo pointer). OpenAI's counter-release: OpenAI then posted its own proof and says it was "obtained on November 6, 2026." Neither lab named a model or published an announcement (@AndrewCurran_). Scope: The result does not imply P ≠ NP, which still requires general Boolean circuit lower bounds (@ZhihuFrontier). Speculation: Curran argues that both labs are sitting on unreleased results and repeats unconfirmed rumors of cryptography breakthroughs. Treat this as opinion. Riemann proof clarifications: Levent Alpöge says the "250,000+ pages" claim was a joke. He released only the Lean code because he could not produce a readable writeup, and called it "full of garbage obviously, but compiles" (@kimmonismus, @simonw). Lineage claim: A Zhihu analysis traces Alpöge's key method to a short OpenAI proof excluding Landau–Siegel zeros. This is an attributed inference (@ZhihuFrontier). GPT-6 protein design, wet-lab validated: OpenAI released a preprint showing GPT-6 models designing new protein shapes and sequences through reasoning and code, without specialized bio models (@OpenAI). Results: 14 of 107 resequenced proteins showed binding. 128 of 182 redesigned small antibodies and 179 of 272 antibody fragments retained binding (details). Cost caveat: On a prior DNA task, GPT-6.1 Sol was about 2,000x more expensive per task than a specialized model (@_lewtun). GPT-6 Cyber and the Linux kernel: In one run, GPT-6 Cyber helped validate 948 Linux kernel bugs that could grant local root and generated patches for maintainer review (@OpenAI). Discovery beyond verifiable domains: A historian says GPT-6.2 Astra identified the vicomte de Chabot as the artist of an anonymous 1808 Yale sketchbook in 22 minutes. It also surfaced an obscure microfilmed diary whose handwriting and itinerary matched the sketches (@HistoryGPT). Exoplanet candidates: Amateurs using Codex and Astra searched Kepler and TESS data. One 13.8-day signal was independently confirmed by a SETI astronomer, and 49 TESS candidates were flagged (@OpenAI). Robotics saturation: GPT-6.2 Astra on Codex scored 97% on RoboDojo-RC Tier 1 across 120 real-robot trials, and RoboDojo is being retired (@robocurve). New environments: Einsia released RoboUniverse-10K, a set of 10,807 verifiable Isaac Sim tasks built from real manipulation videos. The top frontier score on held-out tasks is 85.8%, while 7 of 11 models score ≤10% (@EinsiaAI). Antigravity tokens/day are up 82% since Argon launched six weeks ago (@sundarpichai). Availability: Neon is now available to Google Workspace customers through the Gemini app (@OfficialLoganK). Third-party volume: Perplexity has passed 120B Neon tokens, doubling daily volume in 3 days with 36B on Monday. Arav Srinivas places Neon "between Opus and Fable" in intelligence but best on response style (@AravSrinivas). items.title: Responding to objections to recursive self-improvement
items.summary: (00:00:00) – IntroDwarkesh Patel 00:00:00Okay, so I recently released this essay and this video about recursive self-improvement and why I expect superintelligence by 2030. A wild claim, and understandably, lots of people had objections. Many of them are actually quite interestin
items.details: (00:00:00) – IntroDwarkesh Patel 00:00:00Okay, so I recently released this essay and this video about recursive self-improvement and why I expect superintelligence by 2030. A wild claim, and understandably, lots of people had objections. Many of them are actually quite interesting and compelling, and I want to go through them here. And by the way, I’m joined by Max Farrens, who is my General Manager, and we ended up discussing all of these ideas as we were writing them down. And in fact, we paired in a lot of the writing.(00:00:24) – Jim: “Do you have a real job?”Max Farrens 00:00:25I think a good place to start is with a comment on the Substack version of the post that comes from a user named Jim, who writes as The 1690 Project. “Dwarkesh, do you have a real job where you use this stuff” (meaning AI) “in and day out? I am guessing you do not, because I do, and this is not what I am seeing at all.” What do you think?Dwarkesh Patel 00:00:47Those are two different questions. Do I use these things day in, day out? Yes. Do I have a real job? Debatable. Don’t answer that. Funny that the guy’s like bragging about having a real job. He’s like, he’s like a gotcha on me. Like, I’ve been one of the main people who for the last year and a half has been arguing that the basic learning capabilities that these models lack do in fact impair their productivity. I think people who a naive understanding of what it means to automate a job just look at a system like GPT-6 and say, oh, why can’t we have AGI? It can automate all the white-collar work. I think this is totally wrong. The point I’m making in this essay is that are currently worse than humans at almost everything, right? IT is 1% of the economy, well-scoped coding tasks is a small fraction of IT. In some things, AIs are in fact getting to human level or beyond human level, where we have lots of verifiable proxies. And I would argue that just like math, AI research has a lot of verifiable proxies. And so the consequences of narrow progress in AI research or towards AIs that can do AI research leads to general improvements in AI capabilities. So if you look at a system like GPT-3 and you compare it to GPT-6, GPT-6 is also narrow intelligence, right? It can solve Millennium Prize problems, but it can’t be my video editor. So it can do basically everything way better than GPT-3. What I am imagining is that disproportionate progress in ML research, or AIs that are good at doing ML research, will compress as much progress as we had between GPT-3 and GPT-6 into a single year. And so the end result is within a year of having a system like GPT-7 or GPT-8 or whatever it ends up being, we end up with systems that are more generally capable in the way that humans are generally capable, and are on track to then rapidly become better than humans at everything.(00:02:41) – Cindy Wu: Is AI research a verifiable domain?Max Farrens 00:02:42So Cindy Wu writes on X, “Dwarkesh conveniently sweeps under the rug that climbing a metric involves defining it. Supposing you define it in a way that avoids Goodharting, reward hacking, etc., you need data and environments which do the lifting on defining good metrics. This is most of the game of making AGI, converting fuzzy concepts to formalized objects you can climb without gaming, which requires costly fixes later. He elides the hard problem by saying AI will just automate data.”Dwarkesh Patel 00:03:12I think there’s two parts to Cindy’s objection here. One is: can we find metrics which capture general AI progress? Are we aware of such metrics? And two, will we be able to generate the data that makes AIs good at getting better at those metrics? A big part of my essay was dedicated to articulating what those verifiable proxies for general AI progress are, right? So in pre-training, the loss on a held-out corpus is not only a proxy for pre-training progress, it is the basis of pre-training progress, and that is extremely verifiable. And there’s a lot of other proxies you can come up with that are just general intelligence capabilities that are kind of agnostic for any given paradigm. For example, how fast do you master a video game you’ve never seen before? This is one of the key ways that humans are different from current AIs, that humans master new video games really rapidly. How fast can an AI that has only seen a data corpus up to 1700 figure out general relativity? How many open math problems can it solve, right? So there’s a lot of paradigm-agnostic, hard metrics of progress we can come up with. The second argument here is learning algorithms. The application of learning algorithms is very general. The transformer was invented to beat the existing state of the art in translation, but because that architecture, or the implications of the architecture, were general, it also was really good at predicting the next token in WikiText. It’s also really good at generating images and so on. And similarly with reasoning models. Initially they were

items.title: [AINews] Jensen Is Back! and OpenAI Shows Its Pretraining Curve, joined by Microsoft
items.summary: Congrats to Sierra on tripling last year’s $10B valuation, and to Z.ai for releasing GLM 5.4, their first looped transformer following Thinking Machine’s much smaller Inkling Mini 2 from last week. However all these are outshone by today’s twin title stories… Jensen Huang is back
items.details: Congrats to Sierra on tripling last year’s $10B valuation, and to Z.ai for releasing GLM 5.4, their first looped transformer following Thinking Machine’s much smaller Inkling Mini 2 from last week. However all these are outshone by today’s twin title stories… Jensen Huang is back. Eleven days after announcing his resignation, Nvidia announced his return as CEO, president and member of the Board of Directors. View post on X ↗ The board voted unanimously after more meetings with Jensen on Sunday and said it received input from senior U.S. officials (aka the Treasury Secretary and the President dialing into the board meeting). Colette Kress remains CFO, the independent directors’ investigation continues, and Jensen’s Senate hearing is still due in 8 days. Nvidia also formed a board committee for national security and export control. As Matt Levine points out, with the firing AND the rehiring by this board with involvement from the government, the investigators are now being put in a position of having had the outcome somewhat predetermined for them, because both have demonstrated that they did not need to wait for any further evidence to come to light. OpenAI put its pretraining loss curve on the record. In Perplexity and Intelligence, Chief scientist Jakub Pachocki plotted base-model log-perplexity back to GPT-3.5 (on their internal held-out coding dataset… which has notable caveats): View post on X ↗ Think of it as how surprised the model is by the next token on a held-out dataset. Lower is better. GPT-3.5 was around 0.99 and GPT-4 around 0.91. When OpenAI put a model around 0.76 (GPT6 Astra) to work on open math problems, hundreds of frontier math problems started falling quickly. Pachocki extrapolates that another jump in capabilities could come around 0.68–0.70. This is all in context of pacing the frontier. Pachocki proposes that labs agree on a first limit to development and spell out what would let them cross it, such as a successor to chain-of-thought monitoring. Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman gave the first win by cosigning and joining in, running MAI-2 Base on OpenAI’s evaluation set and reporting 0.819. We’d need at least a couple more top labs to join this effort for it to gather steam as a real self-regulatory limit, most notably of course, Anthropic. It argues for industry-wide limits based on perplexity and other measurements, with further progress gated on milestones in understanding and monitoring AI behavior, such as a successor to chain-of-thought (CoT) monitors (essay thread). Policy framing: Sam Altman quoted the proposal for a first common limit with concrete exit criteria (quote). He tied it to the standards commitments in the White House Accords (accords). Endorsements: Greg Brockman highlighted the warning that alignment progress is unlikely to keep pace with pretraining acceleration (gdb). Mark Chen called the numbers formerly "sensitive IP" and asked other labs to disclose their key metrics (markchen90). Claimed findings: Losses below 0.8 coincided with emergent capabilities in cybersecurity and mathematics (excerpt). Thresholds and timing: OpenAI expects further "transformative capabilities" in the ~0.68–0.7 window and describes a steep acceleration in 2026 (summary). Internal model: An unreleased internal model already sits below GPT-6.2 Astra. Pachocki says pretraining could see an "avalanche" like the recent one in math as soon as 2027 (scaling01). Community extrapolations (unofficial): Dan Hendrycks infers ~3–5×/yr compute-efficiency gains since GPT-4, possibly 100×+ this year (hendrycks). One fit, using the internal model at 0.732 against 0.761 for the released model, reaches 0.70 between January and March 2027 (fits). Microsoft joins: With OpenAI's permission, Microsoft AI reported MAI-2 Base at 0.819 on OpenAI's eval set. It shares OpenAI's tokenizer and lands in GPT-5.6 Sol base-model territory. items.title: [AINews] Riemann Hypothesis proved...twice independently
items.summary: Within a few hours of each other (timeline), two mathematicians claimed independent proofs of the Riemann Hypothesis, the most famous open problem in mathematics (Scientific American). Levent Alpöge of Anthropic first made his Claude-driven proof in a note released with Lean code
items.details: Within a few hours of each other (timeline), two mathematicians claimed independent proofs of the Riemann Hypothesis, the most famous open problem in mathematics (Scientific American). Levent Alpöge of Anthropic first made his Claude-driven proof in a note released with Lean code (1.3GB worth, ~250,000 page equivalent) rather than a full paper. Elliot Glazer confirms that the formalized statement is GRH and puts the chance of a Lean bug well under 1%. So if it finishes compiling with no extra axioms, it is probably correct, and no human will ever have read all of it… …prompting Alessandro Masullo to release his 940 page, 100% human, work in progress proof he had been working on for the last 12 years (and had been undergoing secret manual review and revision per Kevin Hartnett). This is the third in the trilogy of frontier math breakthroughs, following from the Navier Stokes solutions and the Quasi-Riemann bounding, but it doesn’t feel over. OpenAI's September Navier-Stokes claim is still the cautionary tale: critics argued that its Lean proof did not match the natural-language result. Both AI-claimed Millennium Prize results will take years to verify. Apart from the incredible accomplishment of the most famous problem in mathematics, one cannot miss the contrast that the AI-written solution is probably correct but incomprehensible, and the other solution is probably technically incorrect but understandable. Sponsored by Agentfield.AIOpen models are ready. Most coding harnesses aren’t. On DeepSWE, CodeAF finished #1 of ten on the same open model, ahead of Claude Code, at the lowest cost per fix.Try CodeAF! As Levent eloquently put it: “Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.” This also ties into other AI themes we’ve covered on the podcast and on this newsletter: The nature of Slop: Levent says “I am presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics. It being obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of "slop", I decided to only present Lean.” One of the key tenets of the No Slop Manifesto is that you should understand what you ship (“Slop is when we put less effort into producing something than we ask the consumer to spend understanding it.”). And yet, this giant pile of Lean is verifiably correct and is incredibly significant in human history. Should we have delayed its release by a decade simply because we didn’t understand every single bit of it? Weak to Strong alignment: the typical experience of using agents is Strong to Weak - we are general intelligences guiding not-as-smart AI to do things we know how to do well. We also often expect AI to automate most work “within distribution”, and expect it to run into more trouble at the limits of capability where the “centaur” pattern of human-AI-collaboration is required. Levent’s lived experience is the opposite - collaborating with Claude only in the early stages and then leaving him far behind with the critical parts involving automorphic forms on higher-rank groups. We are starting to need Weak to Strong alignment — the open ended domain of controlling AI smarter than us. He says the method also covers the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) (Scientific American, statement summary, remark.pdf link). Artifact: Only Lean code was released. A written-out prose version reportedly ran past 250,000 pages (timeline). Timeline: The work began on Oct 6. Eight of the 20 steps landed on Nov 15, and the final entry on Nov 16 reads "GRH." Alpöge credits Claude for the parts involving automorphic forms on higher-rank groups, an area where he says he has little mastery (breakdown). Unknowns: The Claude model used and the degree of human steering have not been disclosed (open questions). Verification status: Elliot Glazer confirms that the formalized statement is GRH. The Lean code is "still compiling, will take a few hours." He puts the chance of a Lean bug at <<1% (analysis). Provisional status: Artificial Analysis notes that both AI-claimed Millennium results are unverified: this one and OpenAI's September Navier-Stokes claim, which used an unreleased model (tally). items.title: The War Against Slop and an Emerging Weapon to Fight it: Formal Verification
items.summary: The word of the year in the AI industry over 2026 has been “slop” — meaning low-quality output from a large language model. And with so much code being AI-generated now, avoiding slop has become a daily concern for software engineers. So how to do that? One way is to use formal v
items.details: The word of the year in the AI industry over 2026 has been “slop” — meaning low-quality output from a large language model. And with so much code being AI-generated now, avoiding slop has become a daily concern for software engineers. So how to do that? One way is to use formal verification systems, which use mathematical proofs and logic to verify the correctness of software or hardware. With AI’s growing prowess at solving math problems, there’s now a number of AI companies offering formal verification systems. They include Harmonic, Theorem, Axiom Math, and a new entrant called &Truth (pronounced ‘and truth’). In this article we’ll look at some of the approaches these companies are taking. How formal verification is used in software and AI today In order to better understand the landscape of formal verification systems, we spoke to one of its leading proponents: Clark Barrett, &Truth’s co-founder and co-CEO. He’s also Corbel Professor (Research) of Computer Science at Stanford and was the co-creator of cvc5, a popular automated reasoning engine used in formal verification. Without getting too in the weeds, cvc5 is what’s called a “solver” for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT), which Barrett says is widely used in companies like Amazon. For instance, cvc5 is used for specification analysis and test generation in Kiro, Amazon’s agentic development environment. “It's been fun to see my tools go from a good idea in the lab to cvc5 is now called billions of times a day in production pipelines at Amazon,” Barrett told us. Via a 2022 paper about cvc5 co-authored by Clark Barrett. When AI coding agent companies talk about “verifying” their work, it typically means agents running tests, critiquing their own output, or having another AI model judge it. So I asked Barrett how far short of real verification does that fall? “The main difference is really just, how do you know when you're done,” he replied. “So if you're testing, patching, scanning — using all these existing tools — they're quite good. I mean, they find a ton of problems. They raise those issues. But you're never quite sure, did I find all of them [the issues] or is there one more lurking there that my tool can't find?” &Atlas, the first tool of &Truth; it’s “a map of the world’s open-source code, starting with code written in the C programming language.”Lean’s role in formal verification &Truth builds on Lean, an open-source programming language and proof assistant. The company combines AI with automated reasoning techniques to construct proofs that Lean can check. Lean is a language used by frontier models to solve all manner of supremely difficult math problems. For instance, just this week GPT-6.2 Astra produced what Vals believes is “the first Lean proof of Smoktunowicz’s Gap Theorem.” Vals added that Anthropic also used Lean to formalize Fermat’s Last Theorem, a project of 13 million lines. The latest big math news is a report that Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he used Claude to prove the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis — and he posted the proof in Lean. Example of Lean code; via Lean project website &Truth is building what it calls a “verification machine” on top of the Lean framework, with the ambition of reading code “in any language, proving whether it satisfies precisely stated requirements, and enabling humans to trust it without having to understand every line.” “What Lean does is it just checks that you didn't make a mistake,” explained Barrett. “So you can think of it as a very sophisticated checker for mathematics.” This has implications for model training too. Axiom Math uses formal verification to provide correctness feedback for training its mathematical reasoning systems, with proof attempts helping improve future models. In an interview with Latent Space in June, Axiom CEO Carina Hong made the point that formal verification — and what Lean enables — isn’t just a defensive measure. “Formal verification, or verified AI, to us it's not just about handling or kicking out the lousiness, the hallucinations, the mistakes. It's about scaling brilliance. It's about super-intelligence.” Axiom develops AxiomProver, an AI system that generates Lean proofs, alongside AXLE, its toolkit for exploring, validating, and manipulating those proofs. Harmonic’s Aristotle, an “automated theorem prover”, uses Lean heavily in its offering. “Inside Aristotle, AI writes the proofs and Lean checks every step of them, so a result never rests on the AI being right,” states the company on its website. Harmonic’s workflowCybersecurity and LLM-scaled formal verification Given the heightened level of paranoia about cybersecurity these days — some might say in the days leading up to AGI — formal verification systems seem like they’re needed more than ever. And Barrett confirmed that cybersecurity is a key focus for &Truth. “One really powerful use case for our technology is going through all the C code in the world, whether it be open source or cl

items.details: As we previewed on our Know Before You IPO pod, Anthropic set its IPO price at $83 and today $ANT closed at $97.17, up 17% from the offering price (drifting -5% to $92.60 after the close). The $81.3B offering overtook SpaceX's June IPO as the largest in history. Dario and Daniela (Dario’s remarks, Founders’ letter) used the occasion to say Anthropic would pace training and deployment based on whether it could keep its systems safe and under human control. Their Class F shares carry 50.1% of voting power on most shareholder matters. Expect the lockup expiries to weigh on the stock price as about a trillion dollars of shares free up over the next year, while Anthropic has to keep the world’s top model...for now. AI News for 11/18/2026–11/19/2026. We checked 12 subreddits and 544 accounts on X. Search past issues in the AINews archive.AI Twitter RecapAnthropic listed on Nasdaq under $ANT, priced at $83, and opened 34% higher, putting it near a $2T valuation.Listing: Anthropic rang the Nasdaq opening bell (@kimmonismus, @yacinelearning). The official account posted a media-only launch item that drew by far the day's highest engagement (@AnthropicAI). Opening trade: $ANT opened at $111.50, which is $28.50 (34.3%) above the $83 IPO price (@TheRundownAI, @kimmonismus). Pre-open indications were up ~32% at ~$110 (@kimmonismus). Record raise: The $81.3B raised beats SpaceX's $75B (June) as the largest IPO ever (@TheRundownAI). Net proceeds: Expected net proceeds are $104.8B including a concurrent private placement. Fully diluted valuation was ~$2T at the open (@kimmonismus). AMD investment: AMD agreed to invest $2.5B in Anthropic alongside the IPO. The same morning, AMD fell after a Hunterbrook report that a US-blacklisted Chinese server maker kept shipping newer AMD firmware (@kimmonismus, source). CEO statement: Dario Amodei published IPO remarks with a strong safety commitment (details below) (@AnthropicAI). Employee wealth: The average employee could be worth >$40M, per SEC filings and investors (@kimmonismus). Anthropic's 5,300 founders and employees are now worth more than the bottom third of US households, about 45M families (@SteveRattner). Dario Amodei's IPO remarks (official position)Personal framing: Dario and Daniela lost their father to a disease that became curable a few years later. Dario cited CRISPR's decades-long path from discovery to treatment. Core thesis: Powerful AI working with humans "could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade." He stressed that only early results exist so far. Named risks: Misuse by individuals or nation-states, economic disruption, and loss of control. Listed safety work includes bio/cyber safeguards, alignment training, and interpretability ("like an X-ray"). Key commitment: "We will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. We will not bend to either business or political pressure." Strategic framing: The IPO "only strengthens our resolve." He restated the "race to the top," which should work "regardless of whether Anthropic is winning or losing at any given time" (@AnthropicAI). Financials and data points from the S-1 and analystsLow cash burn: Anthropic raised ~$140B and still holds ~$132B on the balance sheet. That implies it "burnt like under $10 billion" to get here, per Tanay Jaipuria (Wing VC) on Latent Space. He called the burn the S-1's biggest surprise, "in a positive way" (@FounderClipsHQ). Bear math from FT Unhedged: A 20% return on ~$1T of compute commitments, at a 40% operating margin and 17% tax, requires ~$602B/yr revenue. That exceeds Alphabet ($471B) and Apple ($478B), and equals two-thirds of the $908B earned by all 76 software/IT companies in the S&P 1500 (@rohanpaul_ai). Use of proceeds: Proceeds are slated largely for data center leasing, which makes SpaceXSI (the Colossus landlord) an indirect beneficiary (@kimmonismus). A critic noted that Elon "rented them an entire Colossus cluster" despite past attacks on Anthropic (@LinusMixson). Google's stake: Google owns 13.7% of Anthropic stock (@NielsRogge). Teortaxes argued Google could still "fumble this by continuing to reinforce Anthropic with TPUs" (@teortaxesTex). After-tax reality check: The median employee likely takes home closer to ~$5M after taxes than the ~$50M headline figures suggest (@futurenomics). Product standing on IPO day: Anthropic is #1 lab on Code Arena WebDev, with Claude Fable 5.2 at 1824, +27 over the next lab (@arena). Arena also posted a lineage visual from Opus 4.5 to Opus 5.5 Max (@arena). Investors and backstoryDustin Moskovitz: The EA funder and major Democratic donor made a critical early bet but is reportedly unhappy, with deep worries about the IPO and fights with Altman, Zuckerberg and Musk (@teddyschleifer). items.title: Scaling Linear’s GTM to $100M ARR — Cristina Cordova, COO
items.summary: Open video on YouTube ↗ Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova, COO of Linear, about how the company
items.details: Open video on YouTube ↗ Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova, COO of Linear, about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation. We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. Half the work on Linear is now created by agents Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents. That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. Cristina thinks SaaS companies settling for that are making a big mistake. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app. So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. If agent usage climbs and app usage doesn't, you're becoming a commodity. At Linear, both are up and to the right, because people still come back to the app to see and coordinate the work. Jump to the MCP discussion →"Issue tracking is dead" When Karri published "Issue tracking is dead" in March, most of Linear's customers agreed with him. Then they asked the obvious question: so what am I buying? Linear's answer is a product development system built around agent orchestration, where humans stop doing the manual work of filing, labeling, assigning and closing issues. Customers had been pushing it there. Most of the frontier AI labs run on Linear and wanted it to move faster. Pre-AI companies like Ramp and Coinbase were building their own internal agents and needed an API to plug them into Linear. Cristina says Linear is lucky it's small enough to cannibalize itself. Google has a much harder problem: put an AI answer above every search result, and fewer people look at the ads. Jump to the "issue tracking is dead" discussion →The AI budget behind $100M in months The thing speeding up purchases right now, Cristina says, is AI budget. Companies carved out money for AI tools that didn't exist before, and any product that fits inside it skips the usual fight for spend. At some companies that budget is very high. It's already starting to change. Buyers are signing one-year deals and paid pilots, not three-year contracts, because nobody knows what they'll want in two years. And some overnight-$100M stories are a handful of $30 to $40 million contracts with defense companies or giant law firms. That's a very different business from Linear's 40,000 paying customers on what was, until June, entirely seat-based pricing. When those one-year deals come up for renewal, we'll find out whose ARR was real. Jump to the AI budget discussion →Linear threw out its 2025 enterprise roadmap Three weeks after joining in 2023, Cristina crossed "move upmarket to enterprise" off Linear's company goals. It had one salesperson. She went after growth-stage companies that would have to rip out an existing tool instead, the same way Stripe won new businesses long before it won switchers. Linear finally declared an enterprise push in 2025, with a roadmap full of features for large organizations. Then agents happened. Linear built an MCP server, an agents platform with a whole new set of APIs, and integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot. None of it was planned, and a lot of the enterprise work never got done. Cristina chose to race ahead anyway. Competitors waited, and enterprises started putting Linear on their shortlists. Jump to the enterprise roadmap discussion →No SDRs, no forward deployed engineers Linear has never hired a single SDR. Cristina thinks the qualification call wastes the customer's time: they want a demo, not questions about their budget. AEs do their own outbound, with tooling to keep it personal. It doesn't do forward deployed engineering either. Linear should be easy enough

items.summary: Is the AI singularity actually coming? Bob McGrew, former Chief Research Officer at OpenAI, argues that superintelligence won’t arrive without changes in the physical world, and that the “hard takeoff” argument is wrong. Sarah Guo and Elad Gil sit down with Bob, an early key exec
items.details: Is the AI singularity actually coming? Bob McGrew, former Chief Research Officer at OpenAI, argues that superintelligence won’t arrive without changes in the physical world, and that the “hard takeoff” argument is wrong. Sarah Guo and Elad Gil sit down with Bob, an early key executive at Palantir who later led research at OpenAI. He is now CEO and co-founder of Arda, which is leveraging AI to make American manufacturing competitive. Bob explains why automating AI researchers is a one-time boost rather than a runaway loop, and why GPUs, compute, wet labs, and factories are the real bottlenecks. They cover Arda’s work with Anduril on everything from actuators to missiles to the Fury combat aircraft, why Arda is building “Cursor for manufacturing engineers”, and how the forward deployed engineering model really works. Plus, the big-picture future view: machines that make machines, self-replicating factories, and Bob’s answer to the Fermi paradox. Sign up for new podcasts every week. Email feedback to show@no-priors.com Follow us on Twitter: @NoPriorsPod | @Saranormous | @EladGil | @bobmcgrewai | @Arda_Industries Chapters: 00:00 – Trailer 00:05 – Bob McGrew Introduction 01:05 – Why work on the physical world during the AI revolution? 02:27 – Why the hard takeoff argument is wrong 05:48 – Labs or startups – who will win in robotics and biology? 13:00 – Why America designs products but doesn’t build them 16:33 – Who needs flexible automation: defense, consumer electronics, data centers 18:19 – Humanoid robots vs. robotic work cells 21:07 – Open-world vs. closed-world robotics 25:20 – Building with Anduril: from days to 90 minutes 28:59 – Palantir’s problem-first approach vs. OpenAI’s technology-first approach 33:15 – From dropping out of Stanford to joining OpenAI 37:13 – Why general robotics models suddenly work 40:28 – Implications for the robotics ecosystem 42:46 – On-device models, speed, and safety 44:18 – How forward deployed engineering really works 50:57 – Superintelligence out of the data center 53:41 – Self-replicating factories and Von Neumann probes 56:46 – Bob’s answer to the Fermi paradox 59:33 – Conclusion

items.title: Cloudflare Joins the Jevolution and Labels Itself a Neolab
items.summary: Cloudflare has been one of the essential infrastructure companies of the web for the past decade and a half. But now, it’s turning into a neolab — at least according to a presentation at AI Engineer Code Summit by Michelle Chen, who runs Cloudflare’s AI Platform on the product si
items.details: Cloudflare has been one of the essential infrastructure companies of the web for the past decade and a half. But now, it’s turning into a neolab — at least according to a presentation at AI Engineer Code Summit by Michelle Chen, who runs Cloudflare’s AI Platform on the product side. We’ll get into what exactly a neolab is in a minute (the short version: they build models and they’re not called OpenAI or Anthropic). Cloudflare is claiming to be one because it too has begun to launch models. Two System One models, to be precise: Clef and Clairic. As Chen explained in her talk, Clef is a decision model directly inspired by TypeSafe AI’s revolutionary Jev model, while Clairic is a new type of system one model that Cloudflare calls an “extract” model. In an interview with Latent Space after her presentation, Chen hinted that Cloudflare won’t just be producing system one models. There will be large language models, too. “We're not being a neolab [to] only launch system one models, even though it makes sense for our infrastructure. We've kind of entered this Pandora's box now, right? We opened it, now the possibilities are endless.” Chen said it’s “not just system one models, but potentially reasoning models that we've been experimenting with, and other LLMs and whatnot.” However, she added that these probably won’t be pre-trained models built from scratch, like the frontier labs produce. “I don't think that's our focus, but I think we can take existing resources out there and make [them] a lot more efficient and effective.” She noted that “most of our team really just does post-training,” so that will be the focus in model development. What is a neolab and is Cloudflare really one? The term neolab literally means a ‘new lab’ and it was coined last November by Stephanie Palazzolo from The Information, who defined it as “a new generation of research-focused AI startups.” Deedy Das, a partner at Menlo Ventures and an AI influencer, runs a big list of neolabs. It includes companies like Thinking Machines Lab, Poolside, and TypeSafe AI itself. According to Das, neolabs employ elite researchers, spend a lot of compute (“usually to train its own AI model”), don't have significant revenue traction, and they’re typically startups that have raised a lot of money. Deedy Das’ list of neolabs — note that TypeSafe is among the top 20. Cloudflare doesn’t tick at least half of those boxes, since it’s a public company with significant revenue traction. In fact, earlier this month Cloudflare announced record earnings. “The third quarter was Cloudflare's best quarter ever,” said CEO Matthew Prince. “We crossed $3 billion in annualized revenue with revenue of $782 million, up 39% year over year.” So Cloudflare as a “neolab” is pushing the accepted definition. However, as Chen argued in her presentation, building models is part of a natural progression for the company: from infrastructure, to compute (e.g. the Workers platform, including now for agents), to storage, to serving open weight models like Kimi, GLM and DeepSeek (on Workers AI), to now building its own models. Jev as the “east wind” Chen readily admits that Jev inspired Cloudflare’s pivot to building models. Referencing a Chinese proverb, she framed Jev’s arrival in September as “the east wind” that unexpectedly changed how Cloudflare viewed AI models. “And so when the system one and Jev paradigm started coming on board,” Chen said in her presentation, “we were like, this makes so much sense for us to adopt, right? We don't have to send every request to an LLM. We can send some of it to a System One model.” In our conversation, Chen commented on how it took only two weeks for them to build Clef — which is a copy of Jev — whereas it took TypeSafe AI two years to build Jev. She meant that as a compliment for how hard TypeSafe AI worked to create this new type of model. “All credit to TypeSafe, really, for actually attacking this space and inventing something new here, that people could relate to so strongly and be able to use it. And, yeah, we came up with a model super quickly, but they put in a lot of legwork and we knew exactly what the API schema should look like and whatnot.” Cloudflare is, at its core, still an infrastructure company — speed and low latency is its meat and potatoes. The main benefit of System One models, Chen remarked, is that they allow more work to be done by smaller, faster models, where output is measured in milliseconds rather than seconds. Clairic and what extraction models do While Clef was a clone of Jev, Cloudflare soon came up with an original twist on System One with Clairic, launched last month as “the first model in a new class: System One extraction models.” “What Clairic does is it can take unstructured input, and it can extract, compute, estimate and forecast values from those inputs,” Chen explained in her presentation. In our interview, Chen said that her team wanted to use System One principles to find other areas where LLMs were “ov

items.details: Perplexity crossed a $1B annual revenue run rate today, CEO Aravind Srinivas told Semafor at a live event. The Information reported previously under $250M at the start of the year and over $750M by August, with Computer driving some of the growth. At usual agent lab multiples (eg Cognition also crossed $1B, with Cursor crossing $4.6B), this would roughly mean that Perplexity is now worth $30-50B — if the unit economics hold up. This is a nice bump on the $20B round in September 2025, and qualifies for our “>$10B fundraise” rule for title stories. Gathering up some recent Perplexity launches for those catching up: Computer. September’s Automations let it pick up recurring tasks where it left off. November’s Teammates take on ongoing jobs. Computer also runs fully locally on supported Macs. Monitor API. Watch a topic or page and get a webhook when something relevant changes. Frontier Research. The new research lab has access to 10,000+ GPUs and plans to publish papers, data, models, and code. Sponsored by DeepgramDeepgram is the voice AI infrastructure behind natural conversation—bringing speech-to-text, text-to-speech, voice-focused LLMs, and agents to teams building with voice AI. For any stack and any tools you already love building with, Deepgram slots in as your foundational voice AI technology. So you have control. And we have the context to listen, understand, and speak like a human.Learn more about the Real-time Context Standard.AI Twitter RecapQwen4-Max in the wild Friday’s Qwen4-Max preview is now a shipping model. At the highest reasoning setting, Qwen4-Max scored 43 on the Intelligence Index, up from 34. Average cost fell from $10.02 to $3.27 per task. Alibaba cut output pricing from $6 to $4.50 per million tokens, and the model generated about 39% fewer of them. Kimi K3.1 Pro cost $3.68 per index task and scored 67% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to Qwen’s 48%. Artificial AnalysisInside the model. Alibaba kept the total parameter count at 2.4T and reduced the number active per token by 25% to 71B. The model takes images and text, with a 1M-token context window. Smaller open-weight Qwen4 models are still to come. AlibabaArena and Vals: Arena ranks it #14 overall on Agent Arena, the top Chinese model, with +7.5% net over 14.7k sessions (Arena). WebDev: It placed #6 in Code Arena WebDev at 1750, +74 over its predecessor (WebDev). It also placed #6 in Image-to-WebDev, just above Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Sol (I2WebDev). Vals Index: It is #11 overall, with large gains in coding and finance (Vals). Legal-benchmark caveat: On HLAB it gets 95.7% of checklist items right but passes only 21.3% of tasks, and its output tokens rise 3.6x (HLAB). Vision results (independent): Roboflow calls it underwhelming on its VLM benchmark, with Google, OpenAI and Anthropic now far ahead. At high reasoning effort, however, it is ~4.5x faster and ~68% cheaper per image than Qwen3.8-Max (Roboflow). Safety, alignment and eval integrityOpenAI embedded assessments: OpenAI is giving Apollo, METR, Transluce and Goodfire internal access to its models and systems (OpenAI). Scope by group: Apollo places six evaluators onsite for four months (Rundown). METR reviews OpenAI's largest RL run, with access to transcripts, monitor records and checkpoint snapshots (METR). Transluce runs a six-week audit of post-training alignment evals, with a fuller follow-up in early 2027 (Transluce). Goodfire embeds interpretability researchers to monitor training runs (Goodfire). Limits: METR says its scope excludes the misalignment incidents OpenAI has disclosed and is narrower than METR proposed (scope). Criticism of the access terms: Critics say the deals fall short of Sam Altman's promise of "employee-like access." Reported gaps: Assessors get no Slack access, OpenAI selects which staff they interview, and they cannot access weights or run training-based elicitation (Neel Nanda, Alex Mallen). Former-employee account: Mikita Balesni says assessors cannot quote employees, even anonymously, and some may be barred from publishing on internal-only models (balesni). Goodfire acquisition talks: The Information reports OpenAI explored buying the interpretability startup for more than $5B. Goodfire reportedly wanted to stay independent so it could sell to multiple labs (report). Other integrity signals: Benchmark contamination: Claude appears to have memorized details of the LinuxArena control eval (Karvonen). Incident taxonomy: OpenAI published a v0.1 framework for classifying AI control incidents (framework). Disclosure policy: Anthropic is cutting its coordinated disclosure window from 90 to 30 days for high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities (policy). Inference systems and agent infrastructureTogether moves on from hand-tuned megakernels. Its first design made it into production for one customer. Agents now search for smaller groups of GPU operations to fuse. Together reports 28% higher throughput on Llama 3.2 1B on B200. Engineering writeupDeepSeek V4.1 Flash

items.details: This episode is sponsored by Deepgram. Try Deepgram for voice agents that truly understand your context! #contextiseverything Not many people know that Stable Diffusion is why I went fulltime into AI (I aptly titled Multiverse, not Metaverse to call out Zuck’s mistaken investment). It turns out that Dustin Podell also had the same aha moment - quitting his day job when the model came out. But we took very different paths… I stuck to what I knew in human content creation, and Dustin immersed deep into AI content creation with Andreas Blattmann, co-inventor of Latent Diffusion and the rest of the world-leading imagegen crew at Stability AI. Stability fell apart, but Anj Midha helped the core group spin out to BFL, which immediately built an incredible new imagegen model in the Flux series. But why are they now going into video and world models? Andreas gives an example you can try with one hand. If somebody tosses you a ball, your hand starts moving before the ball reaches you. You can do that without being able to write down the trajectory. When he talks about building visual intelligence, that’s the kind of knowledge he means. A still can show you where the ball is. A video shows you how it got there. The sound of impact can tell you when it hit something, even if the camera missed the contact. That’s BFL’s argument for training FLUX 3 on the three signals together. BFL’s FLUX 3 releaseThe horse in motion is one of the FLUX 3 examples we show in the intro. The audio examples are worth playing with the sound on. FLUX 3 VideoWhat a moving camera teaches you Suppose the camera starts in front of a person and pans around them. At some point the model owes you the back of their head. Andreas thinks ordinary two-dimensional video contains a great deal of evidence about what objects look like from other angles. That doesn’t settle whether a model “understands physics,” a point we go back and forth on. It does give you a much better test than asking whether one frame looks convincing. There’s a good engineering example late in the episode. Sharpen each frame of a clip independently and each frame might look terrific. Hit play and the extra detail can shimmer, because the upscaler made a slightly different decision every time. BFL derives its video upscaler from the same FLUX 3 backbone. Temporal consistency matters even when all the user asked for was a higher-resolution file. What’s worth spending training compute on? One of the questions I had for them was whether autoregression was taking over image generation. Andreas gives the other side its due. An autoregressive model can learn from all the tokens in a training example at once. On the diffusion side, the team can distill a long sampling process down to a handful of steps. Which advantage matters depends on whether you’re paying to train the model or waiting for an image to finish. Dustin’s early Kontext experiment is a nice example of how they decide where to invest. He suspected an image model that could draw a dog wearing a hat already knew something about where hats go. He and a colleague collected a small set of photos labeled with relationships. A training run of a few hours got the model to put a logo on a shirt. It was rough, but it was enough to take to the next offsite. The team then spent months on the data and the model. FLUX Kontext examples My favorite user story comes near the end. People were feeding FLUX old, degraded family photos, restoring them, then showing the pictures to their families. Dustin says he hadn’t predicted that use. After talking about preserving somebody’s identity across edits and across frames, it’s a lovely example of who actually notices if you get it right. items.details: Paul Christiano is head of the Alignment Research Center. Previously, he was head of AI safety at the US AI Safety Institute. Before that, he led alignment at OpenAI, where he invented RLHF. He’s recently joined OpenAI’s board (though here he is speaking as a private citizen).Paul thinks that on the current trajectory (absent any slowing down), there is a 1 in 3 chance that we could have superintelligence powerful enough to overthrow the government within a year. (He articulates a concrete scenario).He argues that the labs should pause further algorithmic progress until they can secure their weights and research secrets. Otherwise China could simply steal the superintelligence in the middle of the intelligence explosion, and the labs would no longer be able to slow down even if they saw their models going off the rails.He also explains how AIs will be trained during the intelligence explosion, and why even a system trained entirely inside a data center could still have the capabilities profile such that humans would have very little chance of competing with it or controlling it.And he discusses the plan for alignment - basically, making a superintelligence that actually does what we ask the way we mean it. Fixing reward hacks and building better graders will help up till the next few model generations, but he thinks that no single current approach has better than even odds of letting us control superintelligence. The hope is that the AIs figure out the solution to this problem during the intelligence explosion.Watch on YouTube; listen on Apple Podcasts or Spotify.SponsorsJane Street has finally come around on formal methods. Ron Minsky, who co-heads Jane Street’s technology group, told me that up until recently, formal methods just weren’t worth the cost. But coding agents have made them easier to apply AND increased the importance of code verification. So now Jane Street is hiring Formal Methods Engineers in both their London and New York offices. If you’re interested, or if you want to watch my full conversation with Ron, go to janestreet.com/dwarkeshAntithesis is NOT another LLM-based code-review tool. It doesn’t try to reason abstractly about how a PR might break your system. Instead, it just runs your code. You start by defining the rules that your system must never break. Then, whenever an agent proposes a change, Antithesis runs your code through thousands of adversarial worlds, testing whether or not it still adheres to your rules. If you want to try it, go to antithesis.com/dwarkesh and use code DWARKESH for 50% off your first month.WorkOS lets you give agents their own sign-up flow. This matters because agents tend to pick tools they can use right away, rather than ones that require humans to register. Fortunately, providing this kind of dedicated path is easy: if you already use WorkOS for login, you just toggle on “Agent Registration” in the WorkOS dashboard. Once it’s enabled, you can decide what agents are allowed to do on their own, and what needs to wait until the person they’re working for gets involved, all with the permissions you’ve already set up. items.summary: Many thanks to Max Farrens, Gabe Fried, and Thomas Larsen for pairing with me through significant parts of writing and researching this essay. You can watch or listen to me narrate this essay on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts.If you asked me earlier this year how far away w
items.details: Many thanks to Max Farrens, Gabe Fried, and Thomas Larsen for pairing with me through significant parts of writing and researching this essay. You can watch or listen to me narrate this essay on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts.If you asked me earlier this year how far away we are from superintelligence, I’d probably have said at least the better part of a decade. But over the last three months, I’ve updated my views a ton. I’ve been debating people about this question, both on and off the podcast. And I’ve been watching the progress of AI on verifiable domains and thinking about what that implies for AI research itself.I’ve now come to the view that we’re only a couple of years away, and possibly only a couple of months away, from AIs that are as good as the best humans at AI research. I’ve also come to believe that automating AI research will compress so much progress into a single year that, soon thereafter (so by 2030, but plausibly as early as next year), we’ll have AIs that are at least as good as the best human experts in every field. I know this is a wild claim, and it’s one that I myself didn’t believe even a couple of months ago. Let me walk you through how my thinking has changed.Before we get into more speculative arguments, I want to point out that we have a lot of evidence that AI is already dramatically speeding up further AI progress at the frontier.For example, METR, which is an independent evaluation organization, concluded after three months embedded inside Anthropic that Anthropic’s overall rate of progress on well-scoped tasks is 2x what it was a year ago, and that a “majority of this acceleration today is likely attributable to Anthropic’s extensive use of AI to do R&D.”OpenAI published a blog post about this in September, where they showed that the heaviest 10% of AI users among OpenAI’s researchers went from using around $1,000 a day of internal coding agents at the beginning of the summer to over $7,000 a day by the end of August.In September, Anthropic put out a similar post on its own AI uplift. They reported that, as of August, Claude “leads” more than 26% of Anthropic’s AI R&D work—up from under 1% as recently as February.1Math is a preview of what will happen to AI researchWhen I think about how big a deal it could be if AIs automate AI research, and how soon that could happen, a really important update for me has been just seeing how quickly AI capabilities in mathematics have exploded. Current AIs are slicing through well-scoped problems in mathematics like a hot knife through butter. It was only two years ago that I asked Dario why LLMs aren’t able to use their vast knowledge across so many different fields in order to connect different ideas and make new discoveries. And lo and behold, here we are: In a wholly verifiable domain like mathematics, AIs are doing this search-and-match discovery to such a great extent that hundreds of important results (which the top mathematicians and computer scientists in the world had spent decades trying to resolve) are being churned out as side quests to hype up future model releases.It’s crazy how fast we went from, in 2023, “This model can’t reliably add four-digit numbers,” to, in 2024, “This model can barely solve any problems in a high school math competition,” to, in 2025, “Oh, it can win a gold medal at the International Mathematical Olympiad,” to, earlier this year, “Wow, it’s solving open Erdős problems, but maybe just because no human has attempted to solve these particular problems, and a similar solution was already in the literature,” to, about a month ago, “Okay, it fucking solved a Millennium Prize problem in 88 hours.”There’s a line in the novel East of Eden: “And there is one sure thing about the fall of gods: they do not fall a little; they crash and shatter.”It’s true that progress has skewed disproportionately towards the verification-laden parts of math, like finding counterexamples (rather than coming up with new theories, say). Toby Ord posted a great essay about this recently. He writes, “While current AI systems are starting to automate mathematical proof, there is currently very little evidence that they can ask powerful questions or find profound new fields of mathematical enquiry.”But another way to say the same point would be: Current AI systems have solved a Millennium Prize problem, all without the ability to ask powerful questions or find profound new fields of mathematical inquiry.And this ability to solve well-scoped problems is going to be an even bigger deal for machine learning research than for mathematics, broadly construed. That’s because the goal of mathematics research is not just to prove or disprove long lists of conjectures, but to extend human understanding of mathematical concepts. Coming up with the idea of topology, group theory, or the Cartesian grid matters far more than knowing exactly how many one-unit-apart pairs you can make from n dots. items.details: Congrats to Gemini 4 Hydrogen on their launch and it seems Anthropic’s IPO is well under way, but today’s headline was only ever going to be about one thing, the most earthshaking leadership change in AI (after Demis/Jeff/et al at Google DeepMind). Yesterday we covered reports that NVIDIA’s board was preparing to replace Jensen Huang following an NYT report of an affair with an accused Chinese spy. Following news of a second affair, today NVIDIA announced his resignation (correlation/causation is debatable here), presumably forced by the board: View post on X ↗ There is also some discussion of the extent that Chinese models can demonstrably be shown to be trained on Blackwell GPUs that they should not have access to… though the scale is debated. After 33 years, Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO, president and boardmember. Colette Kress, NVIDIA’s CFO since 2013, will keep that job while serving as interim CEO… leading into what will presumably the best attended earnings call in the history of $NVDA next week. AI News for 11/11/2026-11/12/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapGemini 4 Hydrogen: Google's Fast Gemini 4 Tier Ships BroadlyLaunch: Google DeepMind released Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a speed-first model positioned alongside Carbon and Argon. Google says it completes tasks 2.5x faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash and edges Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, 51 vs 50 at default thinking and 54 at the new xhigh level (DeepMind, Koray Kavukcuoglu). Specs and pricing: The model offers four thinking levels (low, medium, high and xhigh) and a 1M context window. It costs $1.50/$7.50 per million input/output tokens, with a 95% discount on cached input (Phil Schmid, Artificial Analysis). Official claims: Google reports 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and more than 3x Gemini 3.8 Flash on Terminal-Bench 4.1. It also claims more than 5x fewer fabricated claims, #1 on Vals Tax Agent Bench and leading results on AutomationBench-AA and Agents' Last Exam (Google). Availability: Hydrogen is available on all Gemini API tiers, including a free tier in AI Studio. It is the default model in Search AI Mode, and free Gemini app users get it through auto-selection. Paid Pro and Ultra subscribers can use it in Antigravity (Sundar Pichai, GeminiApp, Search). Orchestrator multi-model mode: In Antigravity, Carbon plans while Hydrogen writes and tests code. Google says this reaches near-Carbon success on Terminal-Bench 4.0 with 24% less quota and 19% faster completion. It is rolling out to Ultra subscribers (Google, Mohan). Artificial Analysis measurements: The independent results show a mixed profile. Intelligence and cost: At xhigh, Hydrogen scores 54, one point behind Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max) and GPT-6.1 Sol (max). Its cost is about 32% of Sonnet's but about 2.5x Sol's. Cost per task is $3.16 at xhigh and $1.87 at high. Output speed is about 200 tok/s (AA). Strengths: Hydrogen has an 8% hallucination rate on AA-Omniscience, versus 43% for Sonnet and 52% for Sol. It also shares the #1 score on GDP.pdf visual reasoning. Weaknesses: It scores 54% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 at both high and xhigh, below Sonnet at 64% and Sol at 56%. Third-party leaderboards: Agent Arena: Hydrogen debuts at #5 with +14.8% net improvement across 6.5k sessions. It is the fastest model in the top 10 at 5.3 minutes per task median, with a median cost of $1.6 per task (Arena). Code Arena WebDev: It ranks #10 with 1703 points (Arena). Vals Index: It is #6 at 68.5%, 2 points behind Carbon at 38% of Carbon's price (Vals). Coding agents: CursorBench rises to 54.3% from 39.6% for 3.8 Flash (Cursor). Cognition's FrontierCode 2.0 shows 38.2%, just behind Sol (Cognition). SWE-sweep shows 13.5%, versus 9.5% for Astra (KLieret). Caveats from users: Runaway reasoning: One tester saw xhigh spend 131K thinking tokens and about $1.08 without answering a jersey-number image question. The same tester reports budget exhaustion on 1.8% of a text benchmark (skalskip92). Weak spots: Hydrogen scored 1% on MazeBench (patience_cave). Pricing structure: Simon Willison says Hydrogen is only a 25% discount on the Carbon/Argon token price, though those models reportedly double in price on Dec 1 (simonw). Speed: Theo disputes the "built for speed" framing based on his own timings (theo). Open-Weight Releases: Inkling 2 Small LeadsInkling 2 Small: Thinking Machines released the weights under Apache 2.0 (thinkymachines, Mira Murati). Size: It is a 594B-total / 17B-active MoE with text and image input and up to 1M context (HF). Architecture: New components include attention residuals with a q/k/v split, gated attention, a dynamic attention sink, dynamic shortconv and value norm (Songlin Yang). items.title: AI Ambition: ArtCraft Cloned Photoshop and Now Wants to "Rebuild Everything"
items.summary: The theme of day two of the AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco was increasing ambition using AI. And there have been few projects as ambitious as ArtCraft in the AI era. So far the fledgling company has released 17 open source versions of popular software tools, starting wi
items.details: The theme of day two of the AI Engineer Code Summit in San Francisco was increasing ambition using AI. And there have been few projects as ambitious as ArtCraft in the AI era. So far the fledgling company has released 17 open source versions of popular software tools, starting with a Photoshop alternative built from scratch in Rust called PhotoCraft. You could feel the excitement in the room this morning when ArtCraft founder and CEO Brandon Thomas presented a kind of manifesto for AI-based open source at AIE Code. When he mentioned that ArtCraft had cloned Adobe’s Acrobat, with a product called PdfCraft, it got a round of applause from the audience. In wrapping up, his rallying cries of “let's take back the entire internet” and “let's rebuild everything” were greeted with whoops and cheers. Thomas began his presentation by reliving the internet’s early history. In his view, the web started out with the right intentions, but things got screwed up once Web 2.0 hit the mainstream. “We had a bunch of chat applications that were completely open,” he said, regarding the 1990s internet. “So, IRC is like Discord, but you can spin up your own servers that you actually own. You can use whatever programs to automate them and interrogate them without rules.” His point wasn’t necessarily that everything was open source, but that web users could freely build things. With Flash, for example — a commercial animation tool eventually acquired by Adobe — “kids were making all kinds of animations.” When Web 2.0 came along, with its superior broadband and smartphones, “it brought everybody into the fold.” Thomas acknowledged that this widened the scope of internet software, but at the cost of that freedom to build with leading apps. “The diffuse, experimental, early web started to disappear,” he said. “The APIs got taken away from us, and then we started seeing distribution being gatekept by the big providers.” It seems Adobe in particular annoyed Thomas. He described getting billed with an unexpected fee when he cancelled a monthly plan. “It's really frustrating that the web — that was once really, really promising and open and free — has turned into this extractive, owned, rent-seeking world.” This inspired him to start ArtCraft, “with the ethos of ‘let's build everything open source.’” A message even anti-AI people have gotten behind, according to Thomas. In addition to PhotoCraft, they’ve copied other apps in the Adobe suite, cloned Figma, and created a Microsoft-like word processor called WordCraft. There are also independent apps such as SolidCraft, a community-led CAD project distributed through ArtCraft’s launcher. Thomas reiterated that these AI-built applications are 100% open — “not only the desktop apps, but the actual infrastructure as well.” PhotoCraft: The development process ArtCraft is starting with rewriting familiar tools. Thomas’s longer-term vision is for users (such as artists who were previously using Photoshop) to tailor the software to their own workflows. As he framed it, they want to “undo what had happened during Web 2.0, when everything became owned and consolidated and gatekept, and just give people back their applications.” AI is the means to achieve that, he said. But aren’t there already open source alternatives to Photoshop, like GIMP? “GIMP isn't really used by artists,” said Thomas during his presentation. “We actually observed artists vibe coding their own workflows on top of the software that we gave them.” To begin creating PhotoCraft, the team gave an AI model a detailed prompt outlining Photoshop’s tools, data structures and file importers. After that, they “laid out a large, large prompt to say, let's build out the application.” As part of that process, they made everything MCP and CLI compatible. Within 24 hours, said Thomas, “we were looking at a pretty good approximation of what Photoshop was — and it kind of blew our minds away.” PhotoCraft interface; via ArtCraft website Thomas noted that PhotoCraft is “still not at 100% parity” — he said they’ve just passed 60% — but the team has set an internal goal to reach as close to 100% as possible. (The project’s GitHub claims about 76% parity for feature breadth and about 46% for professional readiness.) “Right now, we want to fill the muscle memory of all the artists that use Adobe. So we are going for Adobe, their interface and ‘look and feel’ directly.” But after ArtCraft has achieved that, they plan to “build new apps that have new interfaces that are more agentic.” A big reaction Thomas said he was surprised by the amount of attention PhotoCraft, in particular, has gotten — ranging from the New York Times requesting an interview, to a swelling of its open source community to about 4,000 developers. “I'm still struggling to bear with what has happened. items.title: Powering AI-Driven Drug Discovery with President of Isomorphic Labs Max Jaderberg
items.summary: Drug discovery and development has long relied on expensive, time-consuming empirical trial and error. By shifting the discovery process onto computers, Isomorphic Labs wants to fundamentally change medicine from a process of discovery to one of precision engineering. Elad Gil si
items.details: Drug discovery and development has long relied on expensive, time-consuming empirical trial and error. By shifting the discovery process onto computers, Isomorphic Labs wants to fundamentally change medicine from a process of discovery to one of precision engineering. Elad Gil sits down with Isomorphic’s president Max Jaderberg to discuss his vision for using predictive AI models to achieve experimental accuracy. Max details how the success of AlphaFold provided the first proof of concept that a deep learning model could generalize in the field of biology, and how an AI model’s compounding of learnings allows it to achieve generalizability with scale, thus greatly increasing the probability of success as well as speed in real world clinical trials. He also talks about evolving past the need for animal testing through in-silico models, Isomorphic’s focus on developing drug design engines that are agnostic of disease area, target class, and modality, why accurate molecule engineering unlocks the potential for multidrug cocktails that span complex biological pathways, and how he believes AI molecule optimization will improve both human lifespan and healthspan. AI Twitter RecapGoogle Launches Gemini Decision 1 for Single-Pass ClassificationGemini Decisions API: Google introduced a new API backed by Gemini Decision 1. The model handles closed-set decisions, so it scores choices in a single pass instead of generating text token by token (Sundar Pichai, Logan Kilpatrick, Google). Specs: It supports yes/no, multiple-choice and rubric scoring, with up to 255 multiple-choice options. It accepts text, image, audio, video and PDF inputs, handles up to 1,000 questions per request, has 256K context, returns answers in 150–250 ms end to end, and attaches a confidence score to every answer (@_philschmid). Pricing: $0.10 per 1M input tokens, with $0 billed for output. Google says that is about 5x cheaper than Flash-Lite (Sundar). Origin: The project started as an internal Google DeepMind prototype. A small team shipped the model and API about six weeks later (@_philschmid). Google's comparison with TypeSafe's Jev: Google's own tests show Decision 1 beating Jev 1.14 on 5 of 7 shared benchmarks, including 92.2% vs 90.0% on JevBench. Jev costs $0.042 per 1M input tokens (@kimmonismus). Artificial Analysis evaluation: Independent results are more mixed (Artificial Analysis). Overall score: Decision 1 scores 66 on the Decision Index. That ties Elephant 9B and Jev 1.14, and sits 7 points behind Drex Max v1.1 and GLiDE v1.2. Strengths and weaknesses: It leads AA-Omniscience-Decision (66) and HLE-MultiChoice (49). On AA-Paperclip, it answers every question correctly on only 33% of documents, versus 63% for Drex Max. Cost and latency: It costs $345 per 1M tasks, versus $103 for Drex Max and $156 for Jev. Its Brier score is 0.18. Average time per task is 211 ms, slower than Jev at 92 ms (latency). Early adopters: Stitch built a rapid-design experiment on the API that goes from a rough prompt to a multi-screen product flow in about 5 seconds (Stitch). LangChain shipped day-zero support with a base class shared with TypeSafe classifiers (LangChain). Architecture pattern: At AI Engineer, Cloudflare described a hybrid agent design. Fast decision models handle tool selection and log extraction, and a large reasoning model handles diagnosis only. In its demo, this cut six LLM calls to one and about 40K tokens to 1.8K (TheTuringPost). Frontier Model Evals: Fable 5.2 Leads, Carbon Draws Speed ComplaintsClaude Fable 5.2 on Agent Arena: Fable 5.2 (Max) ranks #1 with a +30.4% net improvement across 4.7K real agentic sessions. That is about 1.6x the score of #2, Opus 5.5 (+19.5%). It is also #1 in Code, Work and Chat (Arena, Pareto view). Pricing: API prices drop from $10/$50 to $8/$40 per 1M input/output tokens. Median cost per task is $7.3, versus $5.5 for Opus 5.5, $1.5 for Gemini 4 Carbon (High) and $6.0 for GPT-6-Astra. Other evals: AA-Robotics v0.1: Fable 5.2 leads at 75, ahead of Astra (69) and Sol (65) (AA). VIALS-AA (visual reasoning): It scores 67% with tools but only 44% without them. Haiku 5.5 with tools reaches 49% at $0.07 per task (AA). Debate benchmark: It won 209 of 224 debates in a Cambridge Union-style contest (@SamuelFitouss10). items.summary: Today at the AI Engineer Code Summit, the main theme was system one models — non-generative models that return structured choices, scores, or probabilities. They’re also typically much faster and cheaper than reasoning LLMs (a.k.a. system two models). And who better to give an in
items.details: Today at the AI Engineer Code Summit, the main theme was system one models — non-generative models that return structured choices, scores, or probabilities. They’re also typically much faster and cheaper than reasoning LLMs (a.k.a. system two models). And who better to give an inspirational rallying cry for system one models than Diogo Almeida, co-founder and CEO of TypeSafe AI. Almeida was lead creator of Jev, the product that kicked off this trend less than two months ago. Jev was an instant revelation for AI engineers when it was released in September. In a podcast with Latent Space on launch (which quickly became our most popular episode of the year), Almeida explained the core problem with making LLMs the heart of software: reliability. In his keynote at AIE Code today, he took it a step further by claiming that Jev is “reliable intelligence” that should be used for “just automating everything.” Integrating system one models into code Of particular interest to AI engineers is Almeida’s point that system one models should become integrated with code. As he put it in his keynote, “code is the language of automation, therefore you need to integrate with code.” Latent Space founder swyx interprets this as a call to “liberally sprinkle ‘System One’ model calls everywhere INSIDE application code to make smarter software instead of increasingly convoluted forms of ‘concat strings together and hope for the best" AI engineering.’” The term “smart software” was used throughout Almeida’s presentation. It sounds like the kind of term used by companies like Microsoft or IBM during Web 2.0, but in the AI era it does actually signify a harsh reality about LLM-driven software: sometimes it’s just not very smart. As Almeida quipped during his presentation, “you get Einstein 95% of the time, but Mr. Bean 5% of the time.” “And if you can't tell which is which, how the fuck are you going to automate anything,” he added. Almeida ended with an impassioned plea to “automate everything.” Like an AI-pilled, pink-haired Steve Jobs, he called out to “the dreamers and the people who don't want to be limited by everything that has happened so far,” promising that TypeSafe AI wants to “really fight for you, and we want this to be as reliable as a fourth logic gate.” How Glean uses Jev With the unenviable task of immediately following Almeida on stage, Chinmay Goyal from Glean presented a more prosaic version of Jev usage. He explained that system one models are used at Glean alongside LLMs and other types of classifiers, and that Jev is especially suited for “zero-shot flexibility.” “As the taxonomy of the decision space changes, we don't have to fine-tune these models again and again,” he said. In a short interview after his presentation, Goyal told Latent Space that their customers don’t actually need to know which type of model they’re using. “Jev powers a significant number of flows [but] the user just needs to have a product that works; that is always our aim with building anything. So we want to hide away all the complexity of whether we are using Jev or we are using a full-blown LLM.” In the conclusion of his presentation, Goyal offered some rules on when to use Jev: Jev patterns and prototypes Next up at AIE Code were Chibi Vikram and Kevin Bernstein from UiPath, a business orchestration and automation platform. One of their examples showed a test of Jev ranking document chunks. They held a “tournament” where Jev picked the most relevant chunks from small groups, then the winners advanced to another round, and so on. This whole process took under a second, even with thousands of Jev calls. “We realized that Jev is a building block that we can adjust,” said Vikram about this and other experiments, “and we have to find these new strategies where we will be able to apply this building block. It might look less intelligent on its own, but with these strategies and patterns, we can get more intelligent — with even the current Jev model that we have.” Scott Roberts, a Principal Engineer at Workday, finished the ‘system one’ session at AIE Code with some prototypes his team has run with Jev. In one, an interface starts to fill in a time-off card while the user is still typing. It was an interesting showcase of Almeida’s idea that a fast model call can change what the software itself does. Roberts described it as going “from predicting what you want to say to predicting what you want to do.” Like the early internet The biggest learning I took from the System One presentations today is that a model like Jev can open up surprising new ways to build software. I was sitting next to a conference attendee who heads up AI at his company. He told me that in his spare time, he used Jev to create a website that sorts and ranks news about fantasy football. But the final word has to go to Almeida, who likened the new opportunities opened up by system one models to the experimentation of the early internet. “I think that there's going to be an
