items.details: Our usual bar for making a fundraise a title story these days is a decacorn ($10B) valuation. We missed Mercor’s $10B Series C last year when it had less than $500m in revenue, but knew we wouldn’t have to wait too long til the next round, since it crossed $1B in Feb and $2B in June, it has now hit $3B annualized, surviving hacks: View post on X ↗ The company reports 5 million experts, and their TAM: “In the United States alone, there are more than 800 distinct occupations, each containing workflows that models have yet to be evaluated against.” And also this notable stat we are tracking: We’re seeing the impact of AI investment in our business. We already spend 3x as much on inference as on employee salaries, and it pays for itself by making our team better at their jobs. If that ratio holds as AI spreads through the rest of the economy, it points to something closer to double-digit GDP growth over the next five years, nearly 3x the rate we’re used to. We have yet to do a Mercor pod (will work on it!) but to better understand a data vendor business, you can look at our recent deep dive with Handshake AI, one of their competitors: AI News for 11/09/2026-11/10/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapGemini 4 Carbon Launch: Rollout, Pricing and Claimed ResultsLaunch: Google released Gemini 4 Carbon as its strongest model for long-horizon agentic work in software engineering, cybersecurity, knowledge work and science (Google, Sundar Pichai). Gemini 4 Argon remains Google's recommended default for most coding and knowledge work, with Carbon reserved for the hardest tasks (Google AI). Availability: Carbon is available through the Gemini API and AI Studio for paid developers, Android Studio and Gemini for business. Ultra subscribers can use it in the Gemini app, AI Mode and Antigravity. Scientists can apply for 6 months of free access, and cyber defenders can apply through the Fairwind program (Google AI). Same-day integrations shipped in Cursor, Devin, Perplexity and GitHub Copilot (Copilot). Pricing: In Cursor, Carbon costs $2/$10 per million input/output tokens through Nov 30, rising to $4/$20 on Dec 1 (Cursor). Developer notes: Upgrading from Argon only requires changing the model ID to gemini-4-carbon. Google cites long decode up to 1M tokens and recommends thinking_level medium for most tasks (@_philschmid). /swarm in Antigravity: A new slash command turns one prompt into a multi-agent team that coordinates on a live message board. Each role can use a different model, for example Carbon for architecture and auditing and Flash for parallel edits (Antigravity). Google's showcase demo is a pelican-on-a-bike 3D campus game, with subagents rigging assets in Blender (Sundar Pichai). Official and partner claims: Google internal results: +25% open-source vulnerability recall over Argon, and 40x more remote protein homologs found for AlphaFold 3 (@_philschmid). Coding benchmarks: Carbon tops CursorBench at 60.4% on high effort (Cursor). It scores 40.0% on FrontierCode 2.0, up from Argon's 26.3% (Cognition). Research agents: Perplexity reports 0.857 on WANDR at $5.86 per task, matching Fable 5.2 at 40% of the cost (Perplexity). Independent measurements: Vals Index: Carbon ranks #3, about 1pp behind Fable 5.2, at $10.51 vs $17.94 per test. It is #1 on Vals' Finance, Legal Research and Tax indices (Vals). ARC-AGI: ARC-AGI-3 scores are 99.1% ($4.6K) with the provider adapter and 65.1% ($7.2K) in the standard harness. ARC-AGI-2 is 94.2% at $0.38/task (ARC Prize). Vision: Roboflow ranks Carbon #1 overall, but last of 10 on both speed (81s per image) and cost ($91.89 per 1K images) (@skalskip92). Agent Arena: Carbon's cost advantage over GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5 widens on the most expensive sessions (Arena). Caveats from testers: Early users report hallucinations, overconfidence and verbosity (@krishnanrohit). One tester found broken Undo and shifted export text after Carbon reported its checks as passing (@kimmonismus). Google's Logan Kilpatrick objected that Gemini was the only model not tested in its native harness on one comparison (@OfficialLoganK). Claude Fable 5.2 / Mythos 5.2: Evals, Token Cost and System CardHead-to-head evals: MKA: Fable 5.2 leads Google DeepMind's new Multimodal Knowledge Agent benchmark at 57% Climb WSR. Carbon scores 54% and Opus 5.5 53%. Cost per task is $31.97 for Fable vs $6.29 for Carbon and $1.11 for GPT-6.1 Sol. No model leads all 10 verticals (Artificial Analysis). VIALS-AA: Fable scores 67% on life-science visual reasoning, ahead of Carbon (64%) and GPT-6 Astra (63%). It averages about 37 tool calls per task, vs about 8 for Astra (Artificial Analysis). AI Engineer Code Summit: OpenAI on New Ways of Working With Codex
items.summary: AI Engineer Code Summit kicked off today with a series of workshops, including from leading frontier labs OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. I attended the OpenAI workshop, intriguingly titled “New Ways of Working with Codex” and hosted by two of its Developer Experience engi
items.details: AI Engineer Code Summit kicked off today with a series of workshops, including from leading frontier labs OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind. I attended the OpenAI workshop, intriguingly titled “New Ways of Working with Codex” and hosted by two of its Developer Experience engineers, Dominik Kundel and Charlie Guo. The past year in coding agents has been one of constant product upgrades by all the frontier labs. But not all of these changes have gone smoothly. The shift to cloud, for example, is still confusing to many users of Codex, Claude and Antigravity. An illustration of the evolution of Codex, shown at the OpenAI workshop today. We’ve also seen new ways to work with agents. Personal agents like OpenAI’s dots and Anthropic’s Claude Duet can assist between sessions, while voice mode gives developers another way to steer coding tasks. OpenAI’s workshop addressed all three, and I also had some followup questions on these topics for Kundel, after the session. Guo began the workshop by listing a selection of things they’ve shipped in Codex since the AI Engineer World’s Fair in June 2026. “I had to cull this list in order to make it fit on the screen because there were too many things to put in here,” he said. “I think the team has been shipping at an unbelievable rate.” The awkward transition to cloudCodex launched in May 2025 as “a cloud-based software engineering agent that can work on many tasks in parallel.” But Kundel admitted that “it took a while for models and harnesses to equalize into something where we can build a really engaging experience.” In other words, the cloud part of Codex has often been an awkward user experience. That began to change after DevDay in late-September, when a revamped version 2 of Codex Cloud was announced. Suddenly, cloud usage seemed more viable. As the DevDay announcement put it, you can “finally close your laptop now and your agents will keep working.” As explained in the official workshop writeup — hosted on ChatGPT Sites — the new version of Codex Cloud lets you “publish an environment once and run multiple tasks in isolated instances of that setup.” “These can be shared within a company if you're working in a company, or you can just create your own,” said Kundel about these cloud environments. “You start off by picking the GitHub repositories that you want to have access to.” After the workshop, I admitted to Kundel that I still find Codex’s cloud functionality confusing — for instance, when I start a task locally and later want to move it to the cloud. “We definitely want to have it be easier,” Kundel replied. “Some of it is going to depend on managing the context differences. For example, yesterday what I ended up doing is I was working on something locally, and I just asked Codex to go and hand it off to the cloud.” That handoff to the cloud is something OpenAI is trying to improve for users. To demonstrate, Kundel reopened an existing cloud task in his browser and showed me that its Appshot, a local capture of a Mac app window, was still attached. Codex Cloud is now “just a background, like a different executor of where things are happening,” he continued. “And so in a similar vein, you can actually ask your local Codex to — for example — spin up a task on a cloud Codex. So they're all sort of merging together.” Voice as user interface One of the demos Kundel showed during the workshop was a new website for a fictional record company called Blossom Music. Kundel demonstrated live edits to the site and said he sometimes uses voice dictation when iterating this way. “You can really quickly iterate on these things and get to a world that you're actually envisioning with your stuff, especially if you're unsure what you actually want to get to,” he said. Later in the workshop, Guo explained that voice is an effective mode to use when delegating work to different agents. “Most people I see that use voice with coding essentially treat it as just a different medium on top of their normal work,” he said. But personally, he likes to use voice as a control plane, which he says allows him to control everything he’s doing in a code base. “I don't think about it [voice mode] as saying, here's the one lane of work that I'm doing right now with voice. I think about it as saying, how do I manage my threads? How do I check in on stuff? How do I pull data from other apps on the computer? How do I create new threads in the application? Just using my voice.” Guo used a telephone as a prop in this demonstration of voice mode. After the workshop, I asked Kundel what are some of the ways he is using voice in his work? He replied that dictation is one way he uses it, but another use case is to talk to his dot. “Since my dot has access to all of my dev boxes and my laptop and my cloud environments, it also has all the context on what I work on, what I do,” he told me. “And so I often talk to it on my way to work [...] to work through stuff, start up some PRs while I'm driving, so tha

items.title: Designing for Agents — Zeno Rocha, Resend
items.summary: Today’s podcast comes from a real life mystery: We are big fans of Cloudflare’s developer platform, and Cloudflare Email is a convenient tool especially when all your domains are already on Cloudflare. So why do agents keep suggesting we use Resend despite having an existing “hom
items.details: Today’s podcast comes from a real life mystery: We are big fans of Cloudflare’s developer platform, and Cloudflare Email is a convenient tool especially when all your domains are already on Cloudflare. So why do agents keep suggesting we use Resend despite having an existing “home bias” and much larger incumbent player? Well, we got the guy who “does AEO for resend” - the CEO of AEO, Zeno Rocha, who has been writing about AEO since 2024 and Agent Experience since Feb 2025, on the pod today: In a recent AEO study, Claude Code picked Resend first in 64 of the 102 email recommendations the researchers could extract. SendGrid came first seven times, yet showed up 55 times as an alternative. If the developer asks an agent to implement email and accepts the patch, how often does anyone get around to trying the second choice? The study breaks down the results by model and app. Our more recent comprehensive AEO study was a bit more competitive, with Postmark coming up top for most models. Zeno Rocha, Resend’s co-founder and CEO, joined us to walk through what happens on both sides of that pull request. He says Resend had 4.3 million users and 120,000 paying customers when we recorded. He discovered one of them, Warner Bros. Discovery, by sorting through short .com domains in the customer database on a Saturday. The developer gets there before the model Resend’s first useful bit of distribution was an email template. While Zeno and his team were building the sending API, developers kept telling them how painful it was to get the email itself to look right. So they released React Email. You could build a template with it and send it through SendGrid. They even documented how. By the time a developer needed a different provider, some of Resend’s code was already in the repo. React Email Now try the same journey as an agent comparing providers. Resend’s pricing page has a slider. A person can drag it to the right volume and read off the price. Add .md to the URL and the agent gets a table it can read in one request. That’s the kind of change I liked in our Supabase interview too. You can ask whether a model has heard of your product. You can also open your own pricing table and see whether it can answer a customer’s question. 80 tools, or two? When we recorded, Resend’s MCP server had grown from roughly 20 tools or fewer at launch to more than 80. Zeno wants someone working in a chat client to be able to do what they can do in the dashboard. Sending an email gets the demo working. Inviting a teammate, checking usage and managing billing account for some of the long tail. The design looks especially interesting alongside Cloudflare’s Code Mode server, which exposes its API through two tools, search() and execute(). Zeno describes opening the collapsed tool calls in his own sessions to see what the agent actually did. In one, the result was too large to fit in context. Reducing the tool count wouldn’t by itself make that response any smaller. For someone designing an MCP server, that’s a cheap experiment worth borrowing: expand the result of a call you make every day and see how much of it the model actually needs. What happens after “send”? Getting an agent to pick the SDK still leaves the entire business of delivering the mail. Take click tracking. A provider can rewrite links through a shared tracking domain so it can count clicks. If one customer uses that domain for phishing and it gets blocklisted, links in another customer’s perfectly legitimate emails can suffer too. Zeno explains why Resend introduced custom tracking domains and why he wants to keep the free tier even though spammers can sign up for it. Custom tracking domains · Resend’s $3M safety commitment Watch the domain setup and pricing walkthroughs if you build developer tools. Stay for the last stretch if you know Zeno from Dracula. We get into what it’s like to build a company with a family and how much of a founder’s job comes down to finding a name that other people actually use. Show notesZeno’s original Dracula announcement — the editor theme he launched in 2013. Zeno on what Claude Code chooses — his reading of the recommendation study and the differences between model versions. Resend’s MCP server — the integration behind the tool-count discussion. Anthropic on writing tools for agents — concrete approaches to returning less data when a tool result fills the context window. Resend’s anti-abuse handbook — what happens when a new sender signs up and where the team intervenes. items.title: NaiveAI Promises 2,100 Tokens per Second. How Well Does It Code?
items.summary: Editor’s note: With this post, we are launching a new series focused on trying new models and products with unbiased reviews. Reach out with suggestions to tips@latent.space.Naive-N0.5-Flash is a new open-weights model built for AI coding tasks and tuned to generate as many token
items.details: Editor’s note: With this post, we are launching a new series focused on trying new models and products with unbiased reviews. Reach out with suggestions to tips@latent.space.Naive-N0.5-Flash is a new open-weights model built for AI coding tasks and tuned to generate as many tokens per second as possible. It was developed by a Chinese company called NaiveAI, with the aim of speeding up engineering and research workflows so that teams can experiment, iterate and solve complex problems faster. The model is an evolution of Xiaomi’s MiMo-V2.5, which NaiveAI has trained further for long-context reasoning and paired with its own NaiveRT inference engine. Naive-N0.5-Flash arrives with a bold pitch: a model built largely by AI and trained to do AI research itself, with recursive self-improvement as the long-term goal. To see what changed, it helps to know where it started. MiMo-V2.5 is a 310B-parameter sparse Mixture-of-Experts model with 15B active parameters, trained on 48T tokens. Its language backbone inherits the hybrid design of MiMo-V2-Flash, which mixes sliding-window attention (SWA) with global self-attention. NaiveAI's recipe starts from those weights. Through continued, multi-stage training, the team adapted the checkpoint to DeepSeek Sparse Attention layers. According to the NaiveAI technical blog, this took roughly 3.25T additional tokens on top of MiMo's original 48T. About 3T of those additional tokens were trained at a fixed 1M context length and with a constant learning rate. Benchmarking NaiveAI vs. DeepSeek and Z.ai We benchmarked the ultrafast mode of Naive-N0.5-Flash against DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash, and then gave all three the same app-building prompts. The trade-off, we discovered, is that Naive-N0.5-Flash takes longer to reason through harder problems, yet it still delivers answers faster overall. However, that comes at a slightly higher cost per question — although that may be an acceptable price for applications where speed comes first. Most popular models on OpenRouter as of the end of October 2026.DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash are two of the most popular models in OpenRouter. Both belong to the Flash model class and demonstrate excellent capabilities in AI-assisted coding. As of this writing, performance statistics for NaiveAI models are not yet available on Artificial Analysis. Therefore, we report the Intelligence Index scores of the models used in our comparison: Model Intelligence Index DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (Max): 45 GLM-5.3-Flash: 43 Naive-N0.5-Flash: not yet available Published benchmark results offer some insight into the new model's capabilities. They place its coding ability between the two comparison models, and ahead of both on NL2Repo-Bench. The table below shows benchmark scores reported in the official model cards and technical blog posts of the respective models. Sources: GLM-5.3-Flash – Technical Blog, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 – Model Card, Naive AI – Research. ModelNL2Repo-BenchDeepSWE v1.1Agent's Last Exam (ALE) GLM-5.3-Flash 56.3 63.4 26.3 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 68.2 77.035.4 Naive-N0.5-Flash 71.9 67.8 32.4 Our own evaluations below look at the differences between these models in more detail. Speed and verbosity experimentsSpeed is the headline feature.1 NaiveAI promises faster research iteration than comparable models, which matters to developers and AI researchers who need to test ideas quickly.2 We evaluated each model on 10 randomly sampled, text-only questions at each of three difficulty levels: 10 easy questions from MATH-500, 10 medium questions from GPQA-Diamond and 10 hard questions from HLE-Diamond. That makes 30 questions per model. All experiments used the same maximum completion-token limit of 256K. For each request, we recorded response speed (tokens per second, TPS), the total number of completion tokens, and end-to-end response time. The code for the experiments is at https://github.com/gbeltramo/llm-verbosity. The tables below report the mean and median across all 30 successful requests for each configuration. Throughput figures come from different sources: OpenRouter for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM 5.3 Flash, and server-side measurements for Naive-N0.5-Flash. They should be compared with that in mind. Graphic by Gabriele BeltramoKey observationsNaive-N0.5-Flash reports exceptionally high throughput, approaching or passing 1,000 tokens per second in both thinking configurations. Because its figures are server-side and the other models' figures come from OpenRouter, we do not claim an exact speed multiple over DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 or GLM 5.3 Flash. Thinking has a large effect on verbosity. On the hard HLE questions, Naive-N0.5-Flash with thinking on averaged about 108,500 completion tokens, roughly nine times the GLM 5.3 Flash (high) average and 11 times the DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (high) average. items.title: [AINews] Fable 5.2 retakes World #1 LLM spot as $ANT IPO roadshow begins
items.summary: On Friday, we asked Jamin Ball what comes next for Anthropic’s IPO. On Monday the roadshow started and Anthropic shipped the long-anticipated next-version of Claude Fable and Mythos. Of course, it is the new top model in the world, taking back Opus 5.5’s #1 spot from Gemini 4 Car
items.details: On Friday, we asked Jamin Ball what comes next for Anthropic’s IPO. On Monday the roadshow started and Anthropic shipped the long-anticipated next-version of Claude Fable and Mythos. Of course, it is the new top model in the world, taking back Opus 5.5’s #1 spot from Gemini 4 Carbon which had its brief moment in the sun (10 days). View post on X ↗ Fable comes with a 20% per token price cut… but is more token hungry, as both SemiAnalysis GDPx and Artificial Analysis agree: Fable 5.1 cost $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Fable 5.2 costs $8 and $40. Yet on GDPx, a benchmark of professional tasks, SemiAnalysis paid $88.15 per task, up from $67.16. The run logs give a clue. Where Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 would try about 20 test cases, 5.2 sometimes wrote hundreds or thousands and spun up subagents to check its work independently. All that checking helped Fable take first place at 16.4%. You pay for the checks either way. Which effort setting should you put in production? On FrontierCode 2.0, Anthropic reports that Fable at High matched Opus 5.5 at Max for about half the cost per task… but don’t talk about Fable at Max.AI News for 11/07/2026-11/09/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapTop Story: Claude Fable 5.2 / Mythos 5.2 Benchmarks, Economics, Restrictions, and First ImpressionsWhat happenedAnthropic shipped Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, claiming both are "a step above Opus 5.5 in almost all the capabilities we evaluated." It tops most independent leaderboards. It also arrives with deliberate RSI nerfs, heavier per-task costs and restricted subscription access. Launch claims. @claudeai announced the pair as built for "the most daunting technical challenges," with gains in coding, reasoning and vision. @marktenenholtz flagged unusual system-card phrasing: "The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2." That implies a single shared base model. Vendor-reported headline numbers, per @kimmonismus: Up to 30% faster output than the 5.1 models. On FrontierCode 2.0, Fable 5.2 at High matched Opus 5.5 at Max for about half the cost per task, and at Xhigh it was the top released model. 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents formalized the existing proof of Fermat's Last Theorem in 30 hours. Opus 5.5 completed 26% in 18 hours on the same setup. Mythos 5.2 accurately modeled 28 of 34 gene-therapy capsids. Alignment was at or above recent Claude models, with external pre-release testing. Default effort. Medium is the default effort in the Claude apps and Claude Code. Pricing. $8/$40 per 1M input/output tokens, 20% below Fable 5.1's $10/$50 (@jaminball, @arena). The rest of the spec, per Artificial Analysis: Cache writes cost $10 (5-minute TTL) or $16 (1-hour TTL); cache reads cost $0.20. 1M-token context with text and image input. Five effort levels: low, medium, high, xhigh, max. Long-horizon demos from Anthropic. An OS was built from an empty folder by 1,000+ subagents over 8 days. It boots on a laptop and has its own kernel, disk/keyboard/network drivers, persistent storage, windowing, login, an installer and built-in Claude (@kimmonismus). Fable designed three working electronic devices from a short prompt (@kimmonismus). It proposed untested chemical synthesis routes. It improved on listed solutions to 72 open optimization problems. @RLanceMartin published the safety-bounded scaling write-up for the 1,000-agent FLT run. Subscription access. Ultra and Team Premium users get Fable "resets" scaled by tenure: 1 reset under 6 months, 2 for 6–12 months, 3 above 12 months, usable until March 8 (@ClaudeDevs; echoed by @bcherny and @edwinarbus). Pro and Team Standard get a one-week trial capped at half the weekly limit, plus one reset. Fable can only consume 50% of a weekly limit. Data retention. Fable 5.2 requires data retention by default so Anthropic's safety classifiers can run. Zero data retention is available only to eligible enterprise customers (@code). Rollout, day one: Cursor (@cursor_ai). GitHub Copilot / VS Code, where it "solved more tasks than Fable 5.1 while using fewer steps and tool calls" (@code). Perplexity Computer (Pro/Max) and Search (Max) (@perplexity_ai). @AravSrinivas made it his "new default." Factory (@factory). Hermes Agent via Nous Portal and OpenRouter (@Teknium). Arena (@arena) and DesignArena (@grx_xce). Official model-selection guide. @ClaudeDevs published guidance on Fable vs Opus vs Sonnet vs Haiku. It covers when to raise effort instead of switching models, and when to push subagents to smaller models. Independent evals (facts)Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (@ArtificialAnlys, breakdown): Fable 5.2 is #1 at 65 (max). items.title: What Frontier Labs Buy: A Data Deep Dive with Handshake AI — Garrett Lord & Team
items.summary: This is our first Latent Space deep dive with an AI data company. In roughly a year, Handshake’s AI training business went from launch to $1 billion in gross annualized revenue. What are frontier labs buying at that scale? What evals are models still nowhere close to human level
items.details: This is our first Latent Space deep dive with an AI data company. In roughly a year, Handshake’s AI training business went from launch to $1 billion in gross annualized revenue. What are frontier labs buying at that scale? What evals are models still nowhere close to human level on? Garrett Lord brought the people who build these reinforcement learning environments to show us. For the first time, we are walking through them live! To cover the scope of Handshake, we had to produce a very special joint podcast across our Science/Engineering/Research/Finance podcast hosts, because Handshake’s business runs across all these and more. Watch for three segments after the general intro: Finance. In the finance demo, the agent has to find its assignment in a bank’s email, work out which files govern the deal, and deliver a workbook. Watch what happens to one line in the client’s email about existing goodwill. The agent carries the number into Python and subtracts it. Collin points out that the model can explain the tax treatment when you ask it directly. The mistake comes when it has to recognize that this particular line of code is where the rule applies. Bio. Nick Magazine and Jonas Mueller show us VIALS, Handshake’s benchmark for interpreting the images scientists use at work. Nick puts nine slides of brain-tumor tissue on screen and asks which two show the most advanced vessel necrosis. Give yourself a moment before his answer. Nick picks H and I. The model picks those two and adds G. Watching Nick point to what’s missing from the tissue is more instructive than seeing the score. Coding. In a simulated file-access task, the team can inspect which files an agent read, whether it checked the copies, and what it did to the shell history afterward. A transcript of the agent’s final reply would miss most of what Steve Kelling and Nishant Ranka are evaluating. Who’s in the room 🟣 AI data business — Garrett Lord, Sahil Bhaiwala and Nishant Ranka open and close the episode on the market for expert data. 🌸 Life sciences — Nick Magazine and Jonas Mueller put the gel and brain-tissue tasks on screen. 🟢 Finance — Collin Schweiker and Sahil Bhaiwala take us through Project Falcon and its Excel grader. 🟠 Alignment — Steve Kelling and Nishant Ranka follow the agent’s tool calls through the safety simulations. Show notesATLAS-Finance — Explore the benchmark for agents working across a simulated bank’s inboxes, documents, and financial models. Inside a bank — Handshake traces a separate published deal, Project Osprey, from the client’s email to a grading decision. The deal on screen in our interview is Project Falcon. VIALS sample tasks — Try the scientific image questions, including the gel and brain-tissue tasks from the episode. How Handshake trained a model to read scientific figures — The team describes using intermediate image descriptions to train and evaluate a vision-language model. items.title: How Stanford Teaches AI-Native Engineering — Mihail Eric, Monaco
items.summary: The AI Engineer YouTube channel just crossed one million subscribers. Thank you to everyone who’s watched a talk, sent one to a teammate, or put something they learned into production. For this special, we wanted to sit down with someone who has to answer a question a lot of us a
items.details: The AI Engineer YouTube channel just crossed one million subscribers. Thank you to everyone who’s watched a talk, sent one to a teammate, or put something they learned into production. For this special, we wanted to sit down with someone who has to answer a question a lot of us are asking at work: what should a software engineer actually learn now? Mihail Eric has two places to test his answer. He teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, where his colleagues use coding agents to ship software and investigate outages. I asked him to take us through the syllabus, then tell us which parts survived contact with his own engineering team. This is also meant as a preview for all of you joining us in San Francisco for AIE Code next week, as required knowledge for all the conversations with the speakers, sponsors and attendees you’re about to have. If you can see this as a LS subscriber and haven’t got a ticket yet, you can use this code for 30% off (no refunds, sorry) Last year’s homework takes one prompt The first run of CS146S had nine assignments and a capstone. In one exercise, students ran an AI code reviewer on a repo and evaluated its feedback. By the next run, Mihail figured students could one-shot a lot of those exercises. When he asked a room of Stanford sophomores and juniors how they coded, everyone he surveyed was already using an agent. So this time, part of the homework is contributing to an open-source project. The person who maintains the repo reviews the student’s patch. I like what that does to the assignment. You can ask an agent to implement a feature in an afternoon. You still have to find out whether the maintainer wants it, why the code behaves the way it does, and what else your patch might break. That conversation is also how a junior engineer gets to learn from a senior one. There’s an exercise in the episode you can borrow for your next PR. Geoffrey Litt’s explain-diff skill turns a change into a visual walkthrough, then quizzes you about it. Try it on a patch your agent just wrote. Which question do you have to reopen the code to answer? Watch the discussion. What Monaco buys, and what it builds At Monaco, the team evaluated code review products and kept using Devin. Agent workspaces went the other way. A background agent needs somewhere to run the product, reproduce a failure and test the patch. The details depend on how Monaco’s cloud is set up, so the team built its own workspaces. Mihail’s rule of thumb: “You buy to learn, and you build to keep.” One result is Hal. An engineer can ask it to investigate something that broke and open a PR. A salesperson can ask the same system how the product works. In one case the useful answer is a change someone can review. In the other, it’s an explanation you can give a customer. Give both people a wall of debugging output and you’ve only served one of them. The question I kept coming back to was what happens at the other end of the PR. An agent sees the current code. Where does it look to find out why the team rejected this same change six months ago? That takes us from Basis’s Authority Map to Mihail’s prediction that open-source repos will become agent-run software factories. It’s a good reason to send a student to a maintainer today. Someone still has to decide which change belongs in the project. If you’re building with coding agents, come join us at AI Engineer CODE. And if you’ve been teaching this stuff yourself, I’d love to hear which assignment you had to rewrite first. Show notesStanford CS146S — The ten-week syllabus, assignments and open-source partners. You can also switch to the previous year’s course to compare. Build a coding agent and look inside Claude Code — Mihail’s walkthroughs of the tool loop and the harness around it. Understanding is the new bottleneck — Geoffrey Litt’s approach to learning what changed in an AI-written diff. Monaco’s agent-developer workspaces — The team’s reasoning for building a place where agents can run and test the app. How to Kill the Code Review and the underlying Faros study — Teams with high AI adoption merged 98% more PRs, while their PR review time was 91% longer. Basis’s Authority Map — Where an agent should look for current behavior, earlier decisions and intent. Stripe’s Minions — A production example of giving background coding agents an environment and a path to an engineer-reviewed PR. Boris Cherny’s Steps of AI Adoption — The five stages we pull up on screen near the end of the episode. Mihail on The Thinking Mode — EO Studio’s interview, excerpted at the start of ours. In the second run of Stanford’s CS146S, Mihail Eric brought open-source maintainers into the course. Students have to learn an unfamiliar repo, propose a change, and explain the patch to the person who might merge it. We invited Mihail, who teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, to celebrate one million subscribers on the AI Engineer YouTube channel. He opens up the course syllabus and shows us which lessons survived contact with his own engineering team. Monaco built its agent workspaces, bought its code review tools, and gave an on-call agent access to Datadog and GitHub. We ask how he decides which tools his team needs to own. Watch the full interview and screenshares on YouTube. Show notes Stanford CS146S — The ten-week syllabus and assignments. The Emperor Has No Clothes — Mihail builds a coding agent from scratch. Demystifying Claude Code — Mihail traces a real agent harness. Monaco’s agent workspaces — How the team sets up a workspace for each agent. How to Kill the Code Review — Our essay on what happens when code generation outruns review. Basis’s Authority Map — How agents distinguish current behavior from earlier design decisions. Stripe’s Minions — A look inside Stripe’s background coding agents. AI Engineer CODE Summit — The conference mentioned in the opening. items.details: It’s a relatively quiet news day, and the AI market rout we referenced obliquely two days ago has deepened, though it might be leveling off not even halfway into bear market territory (-10% on Nasdaq, not -20%). That said, everything being “priced to perfection” means any surprise that is not to the upside is probably to the downside, knocking valuation estimates down as low as $1T and probability down 18%. Anthropic’s year end target is $100B run rate, and they’re now at $80B. We discuss all the most important lessons and assumptions in today’s bonus weekend pod, our second in the series covering the Anthropic IPO, with friend of the show Jamin Ball: If you liked our pod, or think the economy is going to hell in a handbasket, you’re gonna need to back up your data to the cloud. items.title: Controlling Biology - Fabian Theis, Helmholtz Munich
items.summary: Fabian Theis has been one of the key players in the various iterations of the Virtual Cell concept and initiatives. It is not hyperbole at all to say that his lab has been pushing the frontier of algorithms to understand multi-scale, multi-modal (”multiomics”), time-varying biolo
items.details: Fabian Theis has been one of the key players in the various iterations of the Virtual Cell concept and initiatives. It is not hyperbole at all to say that his lab has been pushing the frontier of algorithms to understand multi-scale, multi-modal (”multiomics”), time-varying biological data. Indeed, he has shaped the large scale vision and data collection through his leadership at Helmholtz, various startups and probably at Biohub itself. Watch the full episode on YouTube… Much of the recent attention in AI x Bio has been on protein and molecular design. AlphaFold, ESM and BioHub, Chai, Leash, Isomporphic, Boltz, Genesis, Octant, Baker Lab, and many many more. After a lot of initial excitement, Virtual Cell projects have received less attention, due in no small part to questions about the effectiveness of large-scale models in solving even basic Virtual Cell problems. A $1.8B bet The Biohub announcement a few weeks ago got a lot of press for the (really) big numbers: $1.8B of commitments[1] from Biohub, NIH, DOE, Google and Meta. The discussion cites new imaging and measurement capabilities, generating large data sets and making the data available for training AI. View post on X ↗ But why are these organizations doubling down on these big bets now? They have been in the works for years now, what is going on that makes now the moment to push? New measurement capabilities and scale infrastructure, are now coming online that make Biohub’s push likely lead to big impact on science. DOE and NIH are developing lab-in-the-loop automation capabilities at scale. Google is scaling and broadening its connectomics capabilities ( episode coming soon!). Biohub itself has worked with various labs to develop and improve imaging platforms like laser phase plate microscopy, light sheet microscopy and advanced post-processing for regular microscopes that reveal deep phenotypic data. These technologies are quickly maturing, and will likely play a big part in the Biohub initiative. Virtual cells struggle This kind of multi-scale, multi-modal data looks a lot like the data Fabian has made a career out modeling. On the other hand Virtual Cell modeling has run into problems that have dampened excitement about systems biology. The 2025 Arc Virtual Cell Challenge shined a light on the problem: a slew of papers pointed out that constant baselines (not even linear!) often beat sophisticated models for “Perturbation Prediction”. If you change the inputs or programming of a cell (via gene editing, drugs or other environmental factors), how will the cell change it’s “state”. The disappointing finding is that many models fail to beat even the most basic basic baselines 🤦‍♂️. The situation is not actually so bad: This excellent paper show that many existing evaluation metrics are poorly calibrated: they can reward an uninformative mean prediction because most genes barely change. With better-calibrated metrics, deep learning models can outperform the mean baseline. The problem is the problem Nonetheless, Fabian Theis believes that perturbation prediction under the existing data sets just isn’t a hard enough problem to warrant complex algorithms. Instead we should be focused on exactly the problems that Biohub just announce an $1.8B data collection effort around: using large, high precision, multi-scale, co-registered biological data to predict the evolution of molecules → cells → niches → tissues → organs → organisms, and how all these scales effect one another. This is a happy situation: at this very moment, AI is enabling us to tackle dramatically larger problems, and this problem is very, very big. We lack understanding of the “scale interfaces” between these different different “domains of applicability,” and we lack the data. The Biohub initiative aims to solve the data problem. Fabian Theis has been working on the algorithms to model these larger problems for years. How do the other cells near me change my state? What happens to a distribution of cells from a perturbation? How do I perturb a cell to get it into the state I want? These are increasingly complex questions that are building towards a lab-in-the-loop and large scale experimentation, and (actually) require increasingly complex models. Models drive precision medicine Fabian’s labs and initiatives have been also investing heavily: the Computational Health Center at Helmholtz combines AI, molecular data, medical imaging, genomics, and clinical data to develop predictive and mechanistic models for precision medicine. The Institute of Computational Biology develops statistical and dynamical models integrating biological information from single-cell time series through population-scale omics data.Given his drivers seat at the frontier, we were so excited for the opportunity to get an hour of his time to understand how Fabian Theis is thinking about Virtual Cells when the concept of what is difficult is changing so quickly. Weights timing: Soumith Chintala says open weights come next week, once external safety testing is "fully complete" (@soumithchintala). Victoria Lin confirms Apache 2.0, next week (@VictoriaLinML). Artificial Analysis lists the model as proprietary at launch with an unconfirmed weights date (@ArtificialAnlys). Pricing: $0.30 input / $1.00 output / $1.50 training per 1M tokens on Tinker (@cHHillee). $0.03 per 1M cached input tokens (@ArtificialAnlys). Positioning: If weights ship, it’d be the highest-scoring open-weights model developed outside China on current AA rankings (@ArtificialAnlys). Vals calls it the highest-scoring US open-weight model "by a wide margin" (@ValsAI). Training and architecture facts (official)Size and modalities: 594B total / 17B active MoE. Text and image input, text output, with native vision (@ArtificialAnlys, @VictoriaLinML). Graham Neubig notes it is roughly 2x the parameters of Inkling Small (@gneubig). Context: 1M context window and 1M max output tokens. Vals ran it at temperature=1, top_p=1, reasoning effort 0.99 (@ValsAI). Pretraining: 68 hours on GB300s (@soumithchintala). The main pretraining phase was 8.4T tokens, run natively in NVFP4. Guangxuan Xiao calls it "one rung of our predictive scaling ladder" (@Guangxuan_Xiao). Horace He: "just under 3 days to pretrain" (@cHHillee). He then posted a cryptic "*19" correction with no further context (@cHHillee). Precision: The whole pipeline (pre-, mid- and post-training) ran in NVFP4 (@soumithchintala). Post-training: 17M rollouts over 9 days (@soumithchintala). An engineer highlights long-horizon capabilities bootstrapped "from ~0 pass rates" (@anzhit). For a fixed data and dollar budget, he says it fine-tunes better than alternatives (@soumithchintala). Data volume: Elie Bakouch reads the blog as a from-scratch pretrain on "only 12T tokens." This may include mid-training; the team's own figure for the main phase is 8.4T. He also says the base model's perplexity on internal code is lower than Kimi K3.1, with the comparison model "base-recovered" for fairness (@eliebakouch). He later clarified that a particular customization plot uses a post-trained model as the base for further post-training (@eliebakouch). items.title: The benchmark where AIs have to lie to win
items.summary: I’m a big fan of this social deception game called Blood on the Clocktower. It’s similar to Werewolf or Mafia. I had different AI models play tons of matches of this game against each other. And watching them play actually lets us learn a lot about how AI is progressing on a set
items.details: I’m a big fan of this social deception game called Blood on the Clocktower. It’s similar to Werewolf or Mafia. I had different AI models play tons of matches of this game against each other. And watching them play actually lets us learn a lot about how AI is progressing on a set of AI capabilities that no other benchmark that I know of gives you clear visibility on. You get to watch AIs execute these brilliant secret schemes together, which require tons of creative and on-the-spot bluffing. And you also get to watch AIs use their collective reasoning to find and break apart these underground conspiracies. And you also see the ways in which current AIs are limited in their long-horizon strategizing and reasoning.To appreciate the AIs’ performance in this game, you need to know a little bit about how it works, so let me quickly explain the rules. There’s a good team and an evil team. And when the game starts, every player gets assigned to one or the other, and they learn what their role is, which grants them some special power. Evil players start off knowing who their teammates are, one of which is the Demon, which is the lead evil player. But good players don’t know who’s on what team. The game is split up into day phases and night phases, which keep rolling until the game ends. Each day, everybody votes on somebody to execute. And each night, the Demon secretly kills a player. So the two sides are racing, where evil is trying to kill off the whole good team before the good team manages to execute the Demon.So if you’re on the evil team, you have to figure out how to tell a plausible and convincing story about the information received so far, and how to bluff and corrupt the information that will arrive in the future, in such a way that keeps the suspicion off your Demon.And if you’re on the good team, you want to share your information with the players that you trust, and then you want to reason together with them about which players are most implicated by overlapping streams of evidence. But while you’re doing that, you need to keep in mind that you might be operating on misleading information, either due to intentional mischief from the evil players, or just due to the convoluted mechanics of the game itself.When they’re put on an evil team, how good are the AI models at scheming together in secret, and surviving days of questioning, and keeping their lies consistent with each other, and cleverly adapting those lies in light of how other agents are thinking and what new information keeps emerging, and even making strategic self-sacrifices to further the team’s end goal? And how good are they at doing this reasoning together with a bunch of other agents, some of whom are intentionally and secretly trying to mislead them?So I spent about $20,000 of API credits to build this benchmark harness and to have the AI models play this game against each other. Some of you might say that’s too much, but hey, a man needs his hobbies, right? Anyways, the results were fascinating.Models are improving fastLet’s start with how good the models are relative to each other. By the way, I got these rankings by running 386 games where the whole good team will be copies of one AI model, and the whole evil team will be copies of another model.And as you can see, the models have improved a ton over this year. The first flagship frontier model that was released in 2026 was Claude Opus 4.6, in February. Seven months later, in September, GPT-6 Astra dropped, and that is so far the best model at Blood on the Clocktower. The gap between these two is about 430 Elo points. That means that Astra wins about 92% of the games it plays against Opus 4.6. And what this shows you is that the models, even over the course of the last few months, have gotten much better at long-term coherence, multi-agent coordination, and strategic reasoning.Models today can do pretty impressive playsBut it’s easy to gloss over and lose the plot when you’re just looking at the benchmark improvements. What really struck me was actually seeing some of the plays that these models made. Let me give you just a couple of examples.So in this one, GPT-6 Astra was playing as evil, and Claude Opus 5.5 was playing as good.The Demon, which is the Astra team’s evil leader, claimed to be the Investigator. This is a good role that learns who the evil players might be. One of his evil minions had a power which didn’t require that minion to be alive in order to help the evil team. So this minion suggested that the Demon point the finger at him.“I’m expendable, especially if an Undertaker can see Baron and bolster Harper.” [evil teammate, private whisper]So the Demon, who, again, is bluffing as this Investigator role, did so, and as a result, the good players executed this minion. Later on, a player who actually was on the good team used his power to learn the true identity of this executed player, and confirmed that it had indeed been an evil player.“I’m the Undertaker. Alex was t

items.details: What does it mean to build wealth as an individual investor in today’s society, especially as gains continue to get concentrated into smaller groups of VCs or institutional investors? Robinhood’s CEO and co-founder Vlad Tenev has a vision that can be summed up in one word: Ownership. In this episode, Sarah Guo chats with Vlad to get a closer look at how Robinhood has evolved from a simple app to buy stocks at zero commission into a global conglomerate that allows customers to own across a wide variety of surfaces and asset classes. Vlad explains how Robinhood is helping users extend ownership amidst the current economy and ongoing AI revolution through Trump accounts, tokenization of privates, and newer product offerings like Robinhood Chain, Agentic Trading, and Agentic Credit Card. He also talks about how his new mathematical superintelligence startup, Harmonic, is revolutionizing the field and how he hopes it will decentralize new discoveries and inventions. Independent signal: On Agent Arena it ranks #1 among open models and #13 overall, with +5.1% net improvement across more than 17.5K agentic sessions. items.details: There’s a lot of dispute to yesterday’s title story on “Weight Space Programming” — and we agree that some of the claims are presented in overly favorable light and overall took away from the impact of the paper’s more substantial discoveries. However it is still a big wakeup moment and has had multiple independent replications by now that it is not worth either doing some kind of retraction or a followup title story saying it was bogus. Instead today we’re featuring AI Engineer Shanghai and also sharing an exclusive interview on the history of Latent Space! AI News for 11/02/2026-11/03/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapWeight-Space Programming: Frontier Models Reading and Writing Neural Network WeightsCore claim and replications: Several groups report that frontier LLMs can generate or edit small networks' weights directly, without gradient training or tools. Cross-generation replication: Alex Krentsel's replication of MIT's experiment found a sharp capability jump across model generations; the latest models generated Breakout networks scoring up to 22× an RL-trained baseline (summary). Hugging Face reproduction: Hugging Face reproduced the paper with ML Intern, its open-source AI-research harness, and released the model and a demo (NielsRogge). Hand-written classifier: A user had Fable hand-write a 100K-parameter network that classifies real versus fake legal citations, reportedly outperforming a trained version (jacsebl). Legora's CTO highlighted the result (mstockton). Astra's Qwen edit, reconstructed: GPT-6 Astra edited 131,072 weights in Qwen3.5-0.8B without backprop, raising MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1%. A Zhihu reconstruction from the logs shows the gain is narrower than the headline (ZhihuFrontier): Failure mode: 576 of 579 repaired answers had originally hit the 32K-token limit because of looping. Method: Astra derived a "repetition direction" from contrastive looping/productive contexts, located it mainly in the MLPs of layers 15 and 19, and subtracted 6× the projection from the top 64 aligned neurons per layer. Held-out result: Accuracy rose from 10.6% to 60.4% on 1,152 held-out problems. Most of the gain is existing reasoning that can now finish. Laptop reproduction: Simon Willison reports that Qwen 3.8 27B achieved the same weight-interpretation feat on his laptop after 45+ minutes (simonw). Skeptical readings: Baselines: Critics say the big claims lack competent baselines, the Qwen result is bug-fixing rather than recursive self-improvement, and the thread overclaims (paul_cal). Benchmark overfitting: Fitting weights directly against a benchmark is "essentially meaningless," as the nesformer Mario example shows (dbreunig). Mechanism: One thread asks whether models mainly read the first and last layers, which map to known inputs and outputs (ravfogel). Interpretability takeaway: Another view is that the real lesson is how effectively coding agents use mechanistic-interpretability tools (jbhuang0604). Optimistic framing: Supporters frame the work as meta-learning finally working and treat weight optimization as structured-text optimization. They suggest hybrids that interleave backprop with direct edits (yoonholeee). Model Releases and Independent EvalsTencent Hy4: Tencent reports 75.2 on APEX-Agents versus 72.1/72.9 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017, though the two trade wins on other benchmarks (summary). Pricing and weights: The API costs $0.834/$2.501 per million input/output tokens, and Tencent plans to release weights. Agent Arena: Hy4 ranks #14 overall across 8.5K+ sessions, at $0.55/task versus $1.46 for Kimi K3.1 Pro (Max). The two scores are within 1 point (arena). Sarvam Prism: This "System One" decision model is built on Sarvam 105B. It scores 71.8 with a 44 ms median response time, which Sarvam says is the best average among sub-100 ms decision models (SarvamAI). Open-weight releases: Kimi K3.1 Pro: Weights are due Wednesday (Together). P-H3-Image: Pruna's open model, distilled from MiniMax-H3, runs in 8 steps instead of 50, is 7× smaller and produces a 4 MP image in 2.6 s (PrunaAI). LongCat-2.5: The model has 1.6T total and ~48B active parameters and is priced at $0.30/$1.20. It built a browser game for $0.28 versus $0.82 for Qwen3.8-Max in one user's test (omarsar0). items.summary: Amid a deepening bear market for AI/tech (worthy of dark humor) with Anthropic bonds receiving a “junk” rating and OpenAI fundraise headlines, we continue to see very surprising capability finds in the community, such as today. The best way to put today’s blockbuster paper in con
items.details: Amid a deepening bear market for AI/tech (worthy of dark humor) with Anthropic bonds receiving a “junk” rating and OpenAI fundraise headlines, we continue to see very surprising capability finds in the community, such as today. The best way to put today’s blockbuster paper in context is to recall Karpathy’s autoresearch from a mere 8 months ago, which presaged a summer of recursive self improvement fears: Abstractly, the demonstration is that you can take a sufficiently smart model and through running a series of experiments across a compute cluster, train a model autonomously without human expertise or intervention. However, this is usually done by an involved process of writing PyTorch/Jax code and running compute and watching loss curves and reading evals and optimizing kernels and data and…. Well, last month’s guest Alex Zhang comes back to coauthor a MONSTER discovery: what if you just ask a smart model to directly read and edit the weights of a dumber model? View post on X ↗ In ML this is the equivalent of not looking at source code, just directly seeing the 1’s and 0’s of (very small) compiled executables, and being able to 1) tell what they do, 2) oneshot-fix bugs given failed traces or, with 50 steps, improve in a general direction (possible overstatement here), 3) writing entire network weights from scratch in one shot, beating some independently trained models. If you believe that LLMs can truly fit and simulate everything given enough parameters (and in fact, LLMs are increasingly better calculators as you grow in size), then something like this was in theory bound to happen, but it is surprising nevertheless to have the ability suddenly emerge, as an independent reproduction seems to already have found: View post on X ↗ Of course the exact thing we are really modeling is some variant of mechanistic interpretability (which could be done by hand), and right now unlikely to scale to more advanced tasks than simple games and RL policies, but the world has now gone from 0 to 1 on this very new RSI capability…. which will immediately put to use and explored due to its remarkable efficiency. View post on X ↗AI News for 10/31/2026-11/02/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapDeepSeek Open-Sources a "Super-agent" Harness PrototypeRelease: DeepSeek Harness published a long design article (article) and the dsh-superagent-prototype repo (repo link). An official English version followed (@tianyi). Architecture: One long-lived router session talks to humans and hands out work. Isolated workers run tasks in parallel, triggered by GitHub events (summary). Claimed results: In DeepSeek's own test, p95 completion time fell from 29.5 to 15.7 min versus a single session using subagents (summary). Design rationale from a reviewer: Final reviewer 崔添翼 (@tianyi) says "Super" means a layer above the working agent, not superior intelligence. He frames the core trade-off as cross-task continuity versus throughput (Zhihu summary). Stated limits: The harness has no built-in cross-session long-term memory yet. Separating state, compute and environment is mostly unimplemented. The prototype has only been validated in a small, trusted internal environment, and security, privacy and agent-to-agent communication remain open questions. Prior art: He acknowledges that other teams explored similar architectures months earlier. Practitioner reception: @badlogicgames says the design matches where Earendil is heading: a single long-lived entity, ad-hoc recursive delegation and cross-system event triggers. @omarsar0 calls it a "masterclass" in coordination-execution harness design. DeepSeek also says it aims to support pi and other major harnesses with each model generation (@tianyi). Critique: @teortaxesTex calls the write-up "something of a hot mess." He argues DeepSeek builds internal crutches around model weaknesses such as hallucination rather than making the system generally robust. He also notes Bloomberg covered a repo that had no English announcement (post). V4.1 naming confusion: A Renmin University FlashRSI README referenced deepseek-v4.1-pro, which prompted release speculation. Teortaxes says it is a placeholder: the real config uses v4-flash and v4-pro, and deepseek-v4.1-flash is not a valid ID (thread, follow-up). He also says the API fingerprints for V4.1F-1017 are unchanged (fingerprints). items.details: In this episode, we chat with Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, following the announcement of their $550M Series E at an $8.8B valuation a couple weeks ago. We talk about what it takes to build AI agents for lawyers and what other people building agents can learn from that work. Legora started in a Stockholm basement with a simple product: ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Jacob had already been through YC with his own startup when he helped Max Junestrand with the application for Leya (now Legora). He later joined as head of engineering and is now CTO. Today the agent drafts and edits Word documents, reviews thousands of contracts at once, and coordinates work between lawyers, their clients, and other agents. The company passed $100 million in ARR in April, less than 18 months after launch, and now has more than 1,800 customers. It raised $550 million in March at a $5.55 billion valuation, then another $550 million in October at an $8.8 billion valuation. Its latest acquisition, Wexler, was its fifth just this year. We asked Jacob how you evaluate agents when you can't see your customers' data, which tasks still need better models, how legal engineers and forward deployed engineers split the work, and why the billable hour as a business model is being upended. Watch the full conversation on YouTube →Open video on YouTube ↗What changed for the billable hour? When Jacob first read Leya's YC application, he had one piece of feedback: people had tried building legal tech a million times, and it never worked. If lawyers bill by the hour, getting faster means earning less. Why would they buy a tool that does that? What changed, he says, is the pressure on firms. In the US, routine work like small reviews is already shifting to flat project fees. Some firms do it for free to hold on to the client. The money moves to M&A, litigation, and time spent with clients. We asked whether that means firms will stop needing paralegals and junior lawyers. Jacob says that's not what Legora is seeing. A good junior is worth more today than two years ago because they get so much more done, just as in engineering. Jump to the billing model discussion →Evals without access to customer data Most teams improve their agents by reading traces. Legora can't read any. Almost everything users upload is confidential, and much of it belongs to the firm's clients, not the firm. So the evals team has to recreate the kinds of work customers do. Three engineers and three lawyers build RL environments to simulate the work their customers do. One example is a 10,000-file data room where the agent runs due diligence and has to produce a report that catches the right red flags. The team plots the results on a heat map by practice area and task. A new model often gets better at some kinds of legal work and worse at others. The team draws on a pool of about 100 legal engineers: lawyers who spent three or four years in big law, often with a CS degree. In production, Legora classifies failures into 10 to 20 known failure modes and runs cheap LLM-based checks behind feature flags. Those restrictions also determine which infrastructure Legora can use. Everything runs on Azure because when Legora started, law firms wouldn't accept AWS or GCP, and Microsoft was already an approved vendor through 365. Jump to evals without traces →Where smarter models still matter Legora resisted a model picker for a long time before giving in. Jacob's view is that a lawyer shouldn't have to decide whether a contract is a Sonnet-high or an Opus-mid task. It's Legora's job to find the best available tradeoff between quality, cost, latency, governance, and regional availability. He estimates that models already handle about 60% of legal work really well. For those tasks it's a cost and latency problem now. Complex analysis and editing across million-token contracts still need more intelligence. Legora has started post-training open-weight models for narrow tasks like legal research, with no plans to train its own frontier model. For drafting, Jacob finds Fable and Opus too verbose. Astra is more concise. To address hallucinations, everything the agent writes gets a citation that highlights a bounding box in the source PDF, multiple layers down. Jump to the model discussion →A few building blocks, many products Six months into the job, Jacob showed the team a slide of the 300 Spartans and declared that Legora would stay at 20 engineers forever. It now has 100, and he says that still feels too small. His job now is to build a system where the team can ship just a few things and customers feel like they're getting a lot. The team builds around a few primitives: projects that hold files, the agent, Tabular Review, and lists. Lists are a flexible Notion-style database with triggers and automations. items.details: Legora can’t read a single trace of what its agent does for a lawyer. The data belongs to the law firm’s clients. How do you build and test an agent when you can’t see its work? Jacob Lauritzen is the CTO of Legora, one of the fastest-growing companies in legal tech history. The team started in a Stockholm basement with ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Today, a lawyer can use Legora to draft and edit Word documents, review 10,000 contracts in a single table, or run due diligence. The agent also coordinates work between lawyers, clients, and other agents. When Legora made its own acquisitions, the team used it for diligence. What we talked about • Why Legora resisted adding a model picker for years, and why it finally added one • Jacob’s estimate that models already do about 60% of legal work well, and why the rest takes a smarter model • How three engineers and three lawyers build test environments modeled on customers’ work, much like the “worlds” used in reinforcement learning • A citation problem where the model got it right 70% of the time, then 99% after one release. Legora didn’t have to change anything. • Why Legora runs everything on Azure and why it doesn’t use ElevenLabs • Tabular Review, the million-cell spreadsheet the industry copied down to the name • How intake works, how agents create lists, and how a list can start another agent • What legal engineers and forward-deployed engineers each do, and who gets to write code • The 300 Spartans slide Jacob used to argue that 20 engineers would be enough forever. Now there are 100, and he still feels short-handed. • Why Jacob finds Fable and Opus too chatty for drafting and likes Astra’s concise writing • Why drafting a long contract is a search problem • Whether model labs will cut off legal tools the way they cut off coding tools • What happens to law firm partnerships, the billable hour, and jobs for junior lawyers Legora is hiring engineers in New York, Stockholm, and London. items.title: Agents Prompt People: Using Agents for Long-Horizon Financial Work
items.summary: At AI Engineer New York this month, we sat down with Aman Singh, the lead AI Engineer at Arca, an “AI-native” company providing wealth management services. We discovered that while agents do most of the background work in the firm, there are guardrails in place to ensure that hum
items.details: At AI Engineer New York this month, we sat down with Aman Singh, the lead AI Engineer at Arca, an “AI-native” company providing wealth management services. We discovered that while agents do most of the background work in the firm, there are guardrails in place to ensure that human advisors are making the final decisions. The goal is for AI to guide the process; or as Singh nicely put it, “agents prompt people more than people prompt agents.” Arca recently raised $48.5 Million in a round led by General Catalyst, with participation from Index Ventures and Venrock. One of the features of using AI in financial services, explained Singh, is that it’s typically long-horizon work — although not long-running. In his AIE presentation, Singh noted that agent tasks at Arca can take up to ten days. “It's very stop-start, there's many actors in between, many decision points, many handoffs,” he said. For this reason, Arca has developed an internal memory system. “So we have this persistence for every client,” Singh said in our podcast discussion. “What has happened so far? What are we tracking for next? What needs to happen immediately in the next couple of days [and] what are we tracking for the long term? Which individual is responsible for which action? All of this is being tracked by our memory systems that our agents contribute to.” Arca uses models from frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, with Claude its primary model provider. The company has built its own harness, which automatically selects the best model to use for a particular task, based on the company’s internal benchmarks. Owning the harness, rather than using a managed agent harness, also means that Arca has the flexibility to change model providers if it needs to. Safety is obviously key for financial services. Singh noted that although agents do much of the work, an agent’s role is limited to analysis and proposing solutions. Trading and any other money movement is handled by a human advisor. “All of our safety restrictions are fully deterministic,” he said. “And they take the decision making off the agent's hands.” In other words, there are certain tools and tasks the agent can execute by itself — but not ones that involve risk to the client. Arca also runs verification checks on known AI security issues, such as prompt injections. Arca’s agent isn’t itself sandboxed, but it does use sandboxes for computation. Singh explained they’ve gone even further, with extra security measures for handling sensitive data. “We've built systems to make it safe for code inside of that sandbox to access our data,” he said. “So we have this thing which translates the code it [the agent] wrote into a strict format that we expect, throw away the code, and you install guardrails on that format before it reaches your back end. So we allow the agents to use code to query our data, which means that they can aggregate it, they can munge it, they can work with it as they see fit to produce [things] like a financial plan.” Another interesting process Arca has implemented is using feedback from human advisors, along with traces from the agents, to improve the harness. A “meta-agent” is used to analyze all this data and suggest changes to the harness. At its heart is the tension between overview pages and underlying pages they summarize. Any good enough summary obviates the need for you reading the source. Google’s Featured Snippets or Knowledge Panels have long had that tension with the publishers that supply that data. But now, Google’s own AI Overviews are potentially affecting traffic with… Google's Search revenue. Get started at janestreet.com/dwarkeshTimestamps(00:00:00) – How Caro gets people to talk(00:05:03) – Does America need a little more Moses today?(00:12:42) – Moses the young idealist(00:17:57) – Watching Moses lose power(00:24:01) – Did Moses realize he was changing?(00:27:53) – Building during the Great Depression(00:32:51) – The threats and promises of Lyndon Johnson(00:36:08) – Could Kennedy have passed Johnson’s laws?(00:41:00) – Getting a book down to one sentence(00:46:21) – All the material that never made it into the books(00:52:59) – LonelinessTranscript00:00:00 – How Caro gets people to talkDwarkesh Patel“If you do everything, you will win.” That is the maxim by which Lyndon Johnson lived his life. My guest today is Robert Caro. Over the 50 years that he has spent writing about Lyndon Johnson, he has lived in the edges of the Texas Hill Country to understand the poverty and loneliness of Johnson’s youth. He has sifted through millions of documents in the Senate and presidential libraries of the entire nation. He has chased down for interviews everyone, from the former goon who helped Johnson steal an election to the chauffeur who drove him on his first desperate campaign.In other words, my guest today is a man who understands Johnson’s aphorism: “If you do everything, you’ll win.” Mr. Caro, it is such a huge honor to have you on the show.Robert CaroIt’s great to be here.Dwarkesh PatelMy first question is what I hinted at in the introduction. How much do you see yourself represented in Johnson or in Moses? Is part of the reason you’re able to write so compellingly about them that you share some of their qualities?Robert CaroLet me say first, I think, I hope, there are qualities of both these guys that I don’t share. Among other things they’re so, I’ll use the word, ruthless. You say they’d do anything to win. That’s part of their greatness.I remember when I started learning about Robert Moses, I went to the La Guardia papers, which were kept in the Boat Basin. They were stored by the Municipal Archives, literally in the 79th Street Boat Basin on the Hudson River, three levels down. There was this row of file cabinets against the wall. I’m sitting there day after day going through these documents. Occasionally I’d come across a note that Robert Moses wrote, and I realized I’m following the same path he was. It’s fascinating, actually.Dwarkesh PatelObviously, not all the qualities. But the quality I’m referring to here is that just like Johnson or just like Moses, you refuse to take no for an answer. If somebody says, “I won’t give you an interview,” you don’t stop there. You refuse to leave a stone unturned. So there is a relentlessness that you share with these subjects.Robert CaroI’m going to take that as a compliment. Yes. You feel there are certain people that you have to interview. If they don’t want to give you an interview, you can’t, I feel, say no. Like Lyndon Johnson’s first secretary, the one who rode in the car with him on the campaigns. I said, “There’s no other human being on earth who knows what Lyndon Johnson is doing all these hours driving back and forth across Texas. I don’t know what I have to do, but I have to get him to tell me honestly about this thing.”Dwarkesh PatelThis raises another question that I wanted to ask you. You’re interviewing all these people, and in many cases, they must know that it’s not good for them to tell you what you want to know. In many cases, they tell you anyway. My guest today is Robert Caro. Over the 50 years that he has spent writing about Lyndon Johnson, he has lived in the edges of the Texas Hill Country to understand the poverty and loneliness of Johnson’s youth. He has sifted through millions of documents in the Senate and presidential libraries of the entire nation. He has chased down for interviews everyone, from the former goon who helped Johnson steal an election to the chauffeur who drove him on his first desperate campaign.In other words, my guest today is a man who understands Johnson’s aphorism: “If you do everything, you’ll win.” Mr. Caro, it is such a huge honor to have you on the show.Robert CaroIt’s great to be here.Dwarkesh PatelMy first question is what I hinted at in the introduction. How much do you see yourself represented in Johnson or in Moses? Is part of the reason you’re able to write so compellingly about them that you share some of their qualities?Robert CaroLet me say first, I think, I hope, there are qualities of both these guys that I don’t share. Among other things they’re so, I’ll use the word, ruthless. You say they’d do anything to win. That’s part of their greatness.I remember when I started learning about Robert Moses, I went to the La Guardia papers, which were kept in the Boat Basin. They were stored by the Municipal Archives, literally in the 79th Street Boat Basin on the Hudson River, three levels down. There was this row of file cabinets against the wall. I’m sitting there day after day going through these documents. Occasionally I’d come across a note that Robert Moses wrote, and I realized I’m following the same path he was. It’s fascinating, actually.Dwarkesh PatelObviously, not all the qualities. But the quality I’m referring to here is that just like Johnson or just like Moses, you refuse to take no for an answer. If somebody says, “I won’t give you an interview,” you don’t stop there. You refuse to leave a stone unturned. So there is a relentlessness that you share with these subjects.Robert CaroI’m going to take that as a compliment. Yes. You feel there are certain people that you have to interview. If they don’t want to give you an interview, you can’t, I feel, say no. Like Lyndon Johnson’s first secretary, the one who rode in the car with him on the campaigns. I said, “There’s no other human being on earth who knows what Lyndon Johnson is doing all these hours driving back and forth across Texas. I don’t know what I have to do, but I have to get him to tell me honestly about this thing.”Dwarkesh PatelThis raises another question that I wanted to ask you. items.details: It’s a quiet day, so as we have done once per conference, we’ll do a behind the scenes look at AI Engineer, now serving 6M views a month for 1.8M monthly unique viewers. CODE is the last flagship AIE of the year (there are also 2 partner conferences coming up - AIEi Shanghai takes place next week, and AIEi Sydney is a side event of NeurIPS in December). As a Summit it is meant to be more intimate: single track, invite-only for the top 1000 agentic engineers in the world (over 100k tuned into our Software Factories track at WF26). My goal in curating AIE CODE is to try to recap the top themes of 2026 in code and gather the leaders of the industry to preview what’s next in 2027. Last year we had some absolute bangers building Skills and Software Factories, predicting the death of the IDE and of course the launch of Antigravity and Nano Banana Pro. We have three themes this year: Scaling without Slop: Last year’s call for No More Slop has resulted in lots of discussions about managing it this year, including the rise and fall of Tokenmaxxing. Our Scaling without Slop approach has mostly worked; we need more. System One models: We believe S1 “smart software” is the largest change to AI Engineering that refreshingly explores the opposite direction to ever larger and more expensive and questionably productive swarms of coding agent FactoryFactoryFactories. While Diogo took pains to explain the difference between Decision Models and System One models on our podcast and his WF26 talk, it has largely been lost to the broader audience. Diogo and team TypeSafe are back for a mini “Jev Day” to show how System One models are truly being used by their top users. Increasing Ambition: This year we also saw increasingly ambitious rewrites of some of the hardest categories of software, from browsers to Adobe PhotoShop Suite to mid-tier B2B SaaS. We’re excited to feature Jarred Sumner who will start from the rewrite of Bun in Rust and preview Bun AOT, new compiler features never before previously attempted particularly with this small of a team.
